title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
authors: Jiaming Tang,Zhuoyang Zhang,Junxian Guo,Fangzhou Zhao,Yilong Zhao,Zekai Li,Xingyang Li,Yuyang Zhao,Song Bian,Zhijian Liu,Song Han
abstract:
Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control.
However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable.
We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations.
Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness.
We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use.
We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions.
After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none.
On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort.
Compared with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself.
On LIBERO-Pro, π0.5\pi_{0.5} succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%.
Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks.
These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
introduction:
Robot-use agents (RUAs) have recently become a promising direction for general-purpose robot control (Isola, 2026; Yang et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2026c; Lu et al., 2026).
Similar to a computer-use agent (CUA) that operates a computer from screenshots (OpenAI, 2025a; Anthropic, 2024), an RUA uses a vision-language model (VLM) that observes the robot’s camera images, reasons about the task, and outputs the next end-effector pose.
Because the VLM operates the robot directly, RUAs take advantage of the broad world knowledge and the strong reasoning ability of a capable foundation model, which allows them to generalize and to complete complex tasks.

RUAs built on frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b; Pikus et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a) and Claude Fable 5.2 (Anthropic, 2026) have shown exceptional generalization and language following.
On RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b) and RoboLab (Yang et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026a; SenseNova et al., 2026), agents built on GPT-6 Astra have outperformed the best previous policies.
In contrast, vision-language-action models (VLAs)  (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a) fine-tuned on task-specific demonstrations often struggle to generalize to new goals and follow novel instructions (Liu et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2025; Fei et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Hou & Zhao, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Two factors may contribute to the performance of frontier RUAs: the models have been trained for computer use, and they have strong spatial reasoning abilities.
We hypothesize that the ability to reason in a chain of thought is particularly important for generalization.

However, such performance has so far been obtained only with the strongest proprietary models.
Open-weight models have low success rates on the same benchmarks and fail on some simple tasks as well.
Several works build a harness that adds skills and components such as the segmentation model SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2026) and turns some motions into a small set of options (Yang et al., 2026c; Lu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Chu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Si et al., 2026; RoboDojo Team, 2026).
Such a harness allows open-weight models to complete some of the tasks (Yang et al., 2026c), but it may restrict their action space and thereby make other tasks infeasible.
As models become more capable, some components of the harness may also be absorbed into the models themselves.

Computer-use agents such as OpenAI’s are trained with reinforcement learning (RL) on computer tasks (OpenAI, 2025a; OpenAI, 2025b; Wang et al., 2025), and the close resemblance between the two settings suggests that robot use could be learned in the same way.
We therefore train an open-weight reasoning model with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. To support this long-horizon, multi-turn RURL at scale, we build PEAR (a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics), an infrastructure designed specifically for training RUAs (Section 3.2). In each round, the model observes camera images and the robot’s state, reasons about the task, and outputs the next end-effector pose (Figure 1). Inverse kinematics converts this pose into joint targets, and the robot’s controller executes the movement before the model receives the next observation. Earlier rounds remain in the context, and each episode receives a binary reward indicating whether the task was completed (Figure 2). We provide no perception tools, planners, or skill libraries, so the model itself must localize objects, determine how to manipulate them, and recognize when an action has failed. Because the model specifies poses rather than joint commands and each robot’s own inverse kinematics and controller execute them, the same interface applies in simulation and on a real robot.

Although the model is trained entirely in simulation, the skills it learns transfer well to the real world.
We train the model first on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and then on two tasks in RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026).
On a real dual-arm robot that it never encountered during training, the model then completes 60% of our trials, whereas the base model completes none (Section 4.4).
The checkpoint trained only on the single-arm LIBERO tasks also succeeds in 23% of the trials. These results suggest that simulation-based RL can equip general-purpose reasoning models with robot-use skills that transfer to unseen real-world embodiments.

Our main findings are as follows:

Approaching frontier models on LIBERO. The model improves from 1.6% to 74.4% on LIBERO, outperforms GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a) and GPT-6 Astra at medium effort (48.1% and 49.3%), and closes most of the gap to them at maximum effort (76.2% and 80.6%; Section 4.1).

Robustness and instruction following. The model remains robust when its training tasks are perturbed and follows instructions it has never seen.
LIBERO-Pro (Zhou et al., 2025) changes LIBERO’s goals and layouts, and on this benchmark the model outperforms the VLA π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a) (62.1% vs. 53.3%; Section 4.2).

Zero-shot transfer to unseen tasks and robots. Without any training on LIBERO-Long, the model reaches 39.0% on this suite, on which the base model succeeds in 0.4% of episodes.
On two RoboDojo tasks with a dual-arm robot, the model trained only on LIBERO succeeds in 39.9% and 17.0% of episodes, compared with 10.7% and 13.0% for the base model.
On RoboLab-120, training only on LIBERO raises the success rate from 5.4% to 22.1%, and the model trained on LIBERO and RoboDojo outperforms the π0.5\pi_{0.5} entry on the RoboLab leaderboard (37.3% vs. 28.0%; Section 4.3).

Sim-to-real transfer. The skills also transfer zero-shot from simulation to the real world: without any real-robot data, the model trained on LIBERO and RoboDojo succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot and the model trained only on LIBERO in 23%, whereas the base model succeeds in none (Section 4.4).
Beyond these trials, the model also performs reasoning tasks unlike any seen during training: it draws a simple line version of a painting on a whiteboard and selects a suitable reagent to test whether a solution is alkaline (Figure 7c).

Retained general capabilities. Robot-use training causes no measurable loss in performance on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks (Section 4.5).
This result suggests that RURL can be included as a component of foundation-model post-training.

title: Modeling the Frictional Contact of Continuum Robots with Environments through Linear Complementarity Problem
authors: Jia Shen,Junhyoung Ha,Yue Chen
comment: Accepted for publication in International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR).
abstract:
Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism’s internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption.
This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots. Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications. Experimental validations demonstrated that this model is able to reduce the maximum tip position error from 45.445.4 mm in the frictionless model to 5.855.85 mm in our friction-included model with a 287.9287.9 mm-long tendon-driven continuum robot.

The source code for the proposed model is publicly available at https://github.com/Jia0Shen/LCP-Continuum.

title: Disturbance-Aware Informative Planning in Spatiotemporal Environments
authors: Kaleb Ben Naveed,Haejoon Lee,Anouck Girard,Dimitra Panagou
comment: Submitted to Learning for Dynamics and Control Conference 2027. Project website:this https URL
abstract:
Autonomous robots are widely used for persistent monitoring of spatiotemporal environments, where quantities of interest (QoI) change across space and time and require repeated measurements. In practice, robot motion can be affected by external disturbances that vary across the environment. When such external disturbances are not considered in trajectory optimization, it can lead to inaccurate predictions of robot motion and, consequently, the information acquired about the QoI during execution. However, estimating disturbances throughout the environment can be inefficient, as disturbances in regions with little overlap with monitoring trajectories have limited impact on monitoring performance. We therefore propose a two-stage informative planning framework for unknown, spatially varying but time-invariant disturbances, combining informed disturbance sampling with disturbance-aware trajectory optimization. First, we identify where QoI measurements are needed and generate alternative paths to these locations using the environment geometry. We then prioritize disturbance measurements based on their expected reduction of disturbance uncertainty along these paths. Second, rather than optimizing information acquisition based on nominal robot motion, we incorporate the learned disturbance belief into trajectory optimization to account for its effects on robot motion and information acquisition. Across four simulation scenarios, the proposed method reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.025.0–52.3%52.3\% compared with environment-wide estimation and identifies paths that appear costly under nominal dynamics but become preferable when disturbances are considered. introduction:
Autonomous robots are widely used for environmental monitoring, collecting measurements of quantities of interest such as temperature, water quality, and terrain characteristics (Hitz et al., 2017; Binney et al., 2013; Popović et al., 2020b). In spatiotemporal environments, these quantities of interest evolve over time, causing information decay. Informative planning must therefore account for both information acquisition and decay when optimizing robot trajectories.
A separate challenge is uncertainty about external disturbances, which can affect robot motion and the locations where measurements are collected. Consequently, trajectories optimized using nominal dynamics may acquire less information than predicted during execution.

Addressing these challenges requires accounting for uncertainty about the quantities of interest being monitored and uncertainty about the external disturbances affecting robot motion. Informative planning methods quantify uncertainty in the quantities of interest using measures such as posterior variance, entropy, mutual information, and clarity (Krause et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2007; Agrawal and Panagou, 2023). These measures guide the selection of sensing locations and trajectories through sampling-based planning under travel budgets (Singh et al., 2007; Hollinger and Sukhatme, 2014) or optimization of expected information gain (Hitz et al., 2017; Popović et al., 2020b; Marchant and Ramos, 2014). In spatiotemporal environments, informative planning must account for evolving quantities of interest. Existing approaches use spatiotemporal Gaussian processes (Binney et al., 2013), update sparse spatial GP models online (Ma et al., 2017), or explicitly model information acquisition and decay in ergodic exploration and trajectory optimization (Naveed et al., 2024; Naveed et al., 2026). However, they do not jointly address disturbance learning and its effects on robot motion during informative planning.

Beyond uncertainty in the quantities of interest, other approaches account for the effects of disturbances on robot motion. Popović et al. (2020a) consider localization and mapping uncertainty in informative planning, while Cho et al. (2018) incorporate known wind through direction-dependent travel costs. For unknown disturbances, Sun et al. (2021) use Gaussian processes to learn state-dependent disturbances for safe exploration. Other approaches combine online wind estimation with wind-aware routing (Moon, 2025) or use learned wind maps in quadrotor planning and control to reduce attitude effort (Torok et al., 2026). While these methods address disturbance estimation or its effects on robot motion, they do not jointly consider monitoring-driven disturbance learning and the incorporation of learned disturbance beliefs into informative trajectory optimization.

Selecting disturbance measurements to improve subsequent monitoring requires considering how reducing disturbance uncertainty affects future planning decisions. This is closely related to dual control, which balances immediate performance and learning (Arcari et al., 2020; Li et al., 2025), and task-optimal exploration, which prioritizes learning according to its effect on task performance (Wagenmaker et al., 2021; Wagenmaker et al., 2023). However, directly evaluating this benefit is computationally challenging, as it requires considering possible measurement outcomes, their effects on the disturbance belief, and the resulting changes in subsequent informative trajectories.

To address these challenges, we propose a two-stage disturbance-aware informative planning framework. (i)
The first stage predicts where QoI measurements are needed as information decays and generates alternative paths to these locations using environment geometry. We then prioritize disturbance measurements by their expected reduction of disturbance uncertainty along these paths, weighted by monitoring relevance and accounting for travel cost. (ii)
The second stage incorporates the learned disturbance belief into Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) trajectory optimization, so that the trajectory cost reflects information acquisition and decay along predicted robot motion under disturbances rather than nominal motion. We compare against nominal planning, disturbance-aware monitoring without dedicated learning, and environment-wide disturbance estimation, evaluating monitoring performance over both stages.

title: In Situ Monitoring and Predictive Modeling of Harmful Algal Blooms with Autonomous Surface Vehicles
authors: Nenyi Kweku Nkensen Dadson,Jean Paul Gonzalez,Daniel P. Arabie,Ryan J. Cedel,Dorin Boldor,Corina Barbalata
abstract: HAB (HAB) pose significant environmental, economic, and public-health challenges in coastal and inland water bodies, creating a need for scalable methods to collect spatially distributed water-quality data. This paper presents an autonomous surface vessel-based sensing system for in-situ water-quality monitoring related to harmful algal bloom detection. The system integrates a BlueBoat  ASV (ASV), a motorized winch for depth-controlled sonde deployment, a multiparameter water-quality sonde, side-scan sonar, and an event-camera payload. Autonomous waypoint missions were used to collect measurements across selected sampling regions and multiple depths, enabling both horizontal and vertical characterization of environmental conditions. Field deployments were conducted in Lake Pontchartrain, Louisiana, with additional measurements collected in False River, Louisiana to increase dataset diversity. The collected measurements included algal pigment indicators, nutrient concentration, turbidity, temperature, and other water-quality parameters relevant to bloom formation. In addition, complementary sonar and event-camera data were collected during vehicle operation to provide contextual environmental information. A machine-learning classification approach was also evaluated using the collected water-quality measurements to support  HAB (HAB) and non-HAB classification. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using a modular ASV platform for repeatable, multi-modal water-quality data collection and support future development of autonomous monitoring systems.
introduction:
Algae are often considered as one of the most important plant species on earth; contributing to about 30%30\% to 50%50\% of the available oxygen in the ecosystem [1].
This description of algae is under the wider scope of alga definition. Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are considered as microscopic algae and are widely distributed in aquatic environments across many climate zones. Cyanobacteria blooms may produce cyanotoxins, generate taste-and-odor problems, use large amounts of oxygen in the water and/or create surface scums that degrade water quality. These blooms can be detrimental to public health and are referred to as  HAB (HAB).

Because bloom formation is highly dynamic spatially and temporally, continuous monitoring is essential to support early detection, risk assessment, and timely response. Given the large spatial extent of water bodies, conventional point-based sampling may require an impractically dense sampling network to capture fine-scale variability. This can force a trade-off toward lower spatial resolution. Autonomous robotic monitoring can provide a practical alternative by enabling repeatable high-resolution measurements over such areas, improving the ability to detect, track, or predict bloom formation. Such platforms, including UAV and ASV, have been leveraged for environmental monitoring and marine data collection in recent years [2], but have not been explored for HAB monitoring. To address this limitation, this paper presents an autonomous surface vehicle system for algal bloom monitoring and HAB prediction that integrates repeatable in situ sensing with machine-learning-based identification of HAB formation (Fig. 1). By combining robotic data acquisition with data-driven analysis, the proposed approach aims to improve spatially resolved monitoring and support early assessment of bloom formation in natural water bodies.

title: Toward Resilient Self-Driving Laboratories through Telerobotic Interventions
authors: Ziheng Wu,Adrian Vecina Tercero,Andre A. Fatehi,Abhik Sarkar,Brian Giera,Eric B. Duoss,Christopher M. Spadaccini,Nikhil Deshpande,Aldair E. Gongora
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are accelerating scientific research by integrating robotics, automated experimentation, and machine learning to design and execute experiments autonomously. Fields such as biology and chemistry have shown early success in adopting these systems. However, the increasing complexity of SDLs has heightened their susceptibility to unanticipated faults within automated workflows. These disruptions underscore the need for resilient mechanisms that can effectively address faults without significantly compromising operational efficiency. In this study, we investigate the integration of telerobotic interventions as a solution to enhance the resilience of SDLs against unexpected failures. To address the challenges of fault recovery in SDLs, we developed a teleoperation interface that enables human operators to intervene and resolve laboratory disruptions during automated task executions. The teleoperation interface was designed to allow precise control of a six-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robotic arm (UR3e) using a 3D mouse (3Dconnexion SpaceMouse Pro). Two velocity-based controller strategies were evaluated: (i) a coupled mode, where all six DOFs are mapped to the central knob of the 3D mouse, and (ii) a decoupled mode, which separates translational and rotational motions into distinct controls. To evaluate the framework, teleoperators performed interventions across three distinct SDL fault scenarios. In the first study, comparative trials revealed that the decoupled controller was associated with shorter completion time and reduced rotational motion during teleoperation. In a second study, teleoperators performed an aiming task with and without guidance-providing reference paths. Users were seen to be more target-driven and risk-tolerant without guidance but did show deviations in behavior when presented with different guidance strategies. These findings suggest that controller configuration and reference-path design can influence operator performance during SDL fault recovery tasks, providing insights into optimizing teleoperation interfaces. This work demonstrates the potential feasibility of integrating teleoperation as a human-in-the-loop recovery mechanism for SDL workflows, combining the precision of robotics with the adaptability and problem-solving capabilities of human operators. Furthermore, these findings provide a foundation for future studies in shared autonomy and semi-autonomous intervention.
introduction:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) have emerged as a transformative approach to accelerating scientific research in chemistry, materials science, and biology by integrating robotics, laboratory automation, and machine learning [7]. Due to modern developments in robotics and artificial intelligence, researchers envision SDLs as engines to accelerate discovery where research platforms are capable of autonomously designing and executing experiments with knowledge from subject matter experts and domain scientists. Interestingly, the conceptual foundation of SDLs trace back to the 1960s. Notably, the DENDRAL project [20] developed the first software with predefined chemistry rules to predict chemical structures using mass spectrometry data. By the 1980s, laboratory robotic systems were gaining traction in analytical chemistry, giving rise to early prototypes of what are now regarded as SDLs [24, 30, 25].

With the continued rise of SDL technologies across diverse scientific domains in recent decades, a formal autonomy classification framework has been established to characterize SDL technology. The framework parallels the automation levels for self-driving vehicles by the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) [37]. Specifically, SDLs have been categorized into five levels of autonomy [43, 45, 2, 46]: (I) assisted operation, (II) partial autonomy, (III) conditional autonomy, (IV) high autonomy, and (V) full autonomy. Each successive level reflects an increase in system complexity and integration across both software intelligence and hardware control. A few platforms, such as Adam [47], the BEAR [12], ADA [22] A-Lab [41], and MicroCycle [5], have achieved level IV autonomy, wherein experimental design, execution, and analysis proceed with minimal human intervention.

Progressing toward higher levels of autonomy inherently exposes SDLs to greater demands on reliability, robustness, and adaptability, particularly as the architectural system complexity of SDLs continues to increase. It will require systems that not only operate without human supervision but also recognize, diagnose, and correct their own errors in real time. However, current SDL architectures often presuppose near-perfect automation, relying on tightly coupled hardware-software infrastructures. For example, six-axis robotic arms are frequently hard-coded within highly constrained setups that depend on precise fixturing and predefined placement of laboratory objects [43, 2]. In practice, real-world experimental environments remain inherently variable and prone to disruptions such as robotic misalignments, hardware of software malfunctions, and variable human-system interactions. Beyond degrading performance, such failures can introduce unsafe conditions, including unintended robot motion, material spills, or damage to laboratory infrastructure, thereby posing risks to both human operators and experimental assets. These perturbations frequently interrupt workflows and can lead to cascading system failures, exposing the limited system resilience of current SDL architectures [3, 38]. System resilience, as defined by National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) [16], refers to the ability to continue operating under adverse conditions or stress and recover promptly to support mission needs. Advancing SDL autonomy will therefore require a transition from rigid, deterministic architectures toward adaptive frameworks capable of autonomous fault detection, dynamic recovery, and human-in-the-loop intervention to reduce workflow interruptions and maintain safe operation. Embedding resilience as a foundational design principle will be essential for developing the next generation of SDLs that are capable of sustained autonomous operation.

To address the challenge of enhancing system resilience in SDLs, we consider robotic teleoperation as a promising first step. Teleoperation enables human operators to directly intervene in real time, extending human cognition and dexterity into robotic systems while preserving the precision, repeatability, and stability of automation [19]. Importantly, teleoperation provides a mechanism for mitigating safety risks by allowing humans to respond immediately to anomalous or hazardous system states without direct physical exposure. This is particularly valuable in uncertain or dynamic environments, where autonomous systems may struggle to respond effectively [39]. Fortunately, the concept is well established in fields, such as space exploration, telemedicine, and nuclear operations, that demand reliability under constrained or hazardous conditions [19, 27]. In these domains, teleoperation has served as a bridge between human judgement and machine precision. In laboratory contexts, researchers have also demonstrated the use of teleoperation in a glovebox [44, 21] to mitigate the risk of human exposure to hazardous materials. Building on these efforts, teleoperation represents an underexplored yet powerful avenue for developing SDLs that can recover from unexpected disruptions. Furthermore, recent advances in teleoperation, ranging from optimal control strategies and haptic feedback to immersive virtual and mixed-reality interfaces, have significantly enhanced operator performance and situational awareness through user-centered design [40, 28, 48]. Collectively, these developments position teleoperation as one of the practical pathways toward more resilient SDLs.

Complementing these advances, on-going research has focused on improving the intuitiveness and safety of teleoperation systems through assistive control and guidance strategies [33]. Many platforms utilize virtual fixtures to guide users along the task-specific path and prevents any unintended collision [31]. Compliance-based control schemes, such as those proposed by Bischof et al. [4], combine surface-following and constraint enforcement to implement forbidden regions, dynamic boundaries, and reference path guidance. Nagano et al. [29] designed a guidance system that provides haptic feedback based on trajectory similarity to improve maneuvering performance. Their approach predicts a reference trajectory based on the posture trajectory of the local control interface approaches with predictive displays and semi-autonomous control frameworks further improve user performance by reducing cognitive workload and aid with collision avoidance [9, 35]. Yet, few studies evaluated the selection of these reference paths. Meanwhile, Gottardi et al. [13] proposed a shared-control framework that assists operators to navigate between static and dynamic obstacles. Using the improved potential field method, their system dynamically generates escape waypoints which serve as attractors to the teleoperation path. Collectively, these contributions highlight a robust foundation for integration of advanced teleoperation methodologies into SDLs, paving the way for hybrid systems that blend autonomy with adaptive human oversight.

Current SDLs often lack teleoperation-assisted recovery mechanisms that allow humans to safely and efficiently intervene when unexpected faults arise. The goal of this work is not to introduce a fundamentally new teleoperation algorithm, but rather to investigate how teleoperation can be leveraged to strengthen the system resilience of SDLs by enabling human-guided fault recovery.

We first discuss the development of telerobotic capabilities, building upon prior advances in teleoperation interface design and control, to create an intuitive and adaptive human–machine collaboration environment. The system centers on a six-axis robotic arm controlled via a 3D input device, employing velocity-based motion mapping for precise and responsive real-time manipulation. Among available teleoperation interfaces, the 3D SpaceMouse offers a cost-effective and widely adopted solution for achieving fine-grained spatial control [17, 23, 34]. We then evaluate control strategies for telerobotic operation through a preliminary user study, quantifying the trade-offs among different velocity-based control modes and their influence on user performance during representative SDL fault recovery tasks.

To further assess how teleoperation can improve operator performance, we implement another user study to investigate the effect of reference-path guidance, analyzing how trajectory design affects teleoperator performance. From selected teleoperated trajectories, we retrospectively analyze collision and singularity risk using three quantitative indices that characterize controllability, system responsiveness, and motion stability, providing a principled basis for mitigating self-entanglement and improving task efficiency.

Finally, we integrate these telerobotic capabilities into a real-world SDL setup for a qualitative demonstration, illustrating how human-in-the-loop fault recovery could significantly improve laboratory uptime and operational robustness. Collectively, these studies establish a quantitative, qualitative, and experimental foundation for teleoperation-assisted fault recovery, marking a step toward resilient, adaptive, and fault-tolerant SDLs capable of sustained operation under real-world uncertainty.

title: When Will You Hand It Over? A Hidden Start Delay Makes Self-Play Handover Robust to Unfamiliar Partners
authors: Mohammad Khoshnazar,Mike Degany,Deyuan Qu,Qing Yang,Matyas Szanto

abstract: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35–41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.
introduction:
A handover is a joint action. Giver and receiver must agree not only on where the object changes hands but on when: the receiver has to arrive, take the weight and keep the object supported while the giver lets go, and each side times its part on the other [18, 13]. A robot that receives objects from people therefore faces givers who start when they are ready, not when the robot expects them to: a human-induced distribution shift that a learned policy must absorb.

Cooperative self-play is an attractive way to learn this coordination, because it needs no demonstrations: a receiver and a giver are trained together and discover a fluent exchange. But a policy pair that is fluent with itself may have agreed on a private convention, a failure known from cooperative games [5, 2]. Whether such conventions arise in contact-rich physical handover, what they consist of, and how to remove them has not been established. We study these questions in a physics-based parcel handover between a fixed-base Unitree G1 and a learned, human-constrained partner (Figure 1).

The convention exists, and it is temporal. The self-play receiver succeeds in 95.0 / 89.5% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but in only 30.5 / 30.5% with scripted partners it has never met. We trace this collapse mainly to one variable, the moment the partner starts. Because the partner shares the receiver’s reward, it always starts its offer immediately, and the receiver learns to take the parcel on the fly at a fixed moment of the partner’s reach. Delaying the receiver’s own partner by one second, with everything else unchanged, reproduces the failure (95% to 6%, and 87% to 34%); making a scripted partner prompt and smooth removes most of it.

The diagnosis yields a simple and effective repair. Hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD) keeps the learned partner’s hand at rest for a hidden, per-episode time before it may begin to offer; the receiver’s observations, rewards and network are untouched. After 300 further updates the receiver reaches 80.5 / 80.0% with unseen scripted partners, 2.6 times its previous level, while a budget-matched continuation without HSD stays at 35.0 / 41.0%. The robustness extends to a fresh scenario seed, to eleven held-out partner conditions and to partners that start later than any delay seen in training.

(i) CoPlay-Handover, a physically coupled two-policy handover framework in which the giver’s offer and release are learned, together with a support-aware success measure (Figure 2). (ii) A causal diagnosis by paired interventions: the failure of self-play handover with unfamiliar partners is caused mainly by partner start timing, not by partner identity or by the partner’s fine corrections. (iii) HSD, a hidden constraint on the partner that repairs the failure, validated against a matched control, on a fresh scenario seed, on held-out conditions and with a frozen partner. (iv) A second hidden rule, on release, that teaches the receiver to hold still for partners that require it.

title: The State Is Not the Bottleneck: A Paged-State Gated-DeltaNet Tile on a Tri-Mode Multicast Mesh, Bit-Exact from RTL to Silicon

abstract:
Linear-attention language models replace a growing key–value cache with a recurrent state of fixed size.
On an edge FPGA, this state can exceed the on-chip memory and must be paged to external memory.
This paper asks whether such paging dominates the cost of decoding (generating tokens).
We built a hardware tile that computes one complete layer of a custom 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model on an Agilex 5 FPGA and pages its recurrent state.
The model state needs 6.2 MiB, whereas the device has 0.87 MiB of block memory.
Paging adds 26.0 MB of memory traffic per decoded token, at most 11.2 percent of the calculated total.
On the board at 75 MHz, with synthetic weights, one token takes 11.15 ms in this layer.
The matrix-vector products with the weights take about 62 percent of this time and the state phase, including the paging, 13 percent.
The tile is one node of a multicast mesh of tri-mode processing elements.
We measure the error of the fixed-point arithmetic against floating point and check that the hardware agrees bit for bit with a fixed-point reference.
In simulation, the state logic agrees with the reference on all 18 recurrent layers.
On the board, six builds pass all 30 runs of 64 tokens and two runs of 1,024 tokens.
For this model and memory interface, the delivery of the weights limits the decoding performance, and the recurrent state does not.
State paging is therefore practical for such a model on an edge FPGA.
introduction:
Linear attention replaces the growing key–value (KV) cache of a transformer language model with a recurrent state of fixed size [1, 2].
This state can still be larger than the on-chip memory of an edge FPGA.
Our custom model, a hybrid of the Gated DeltaNet type [2], has 369 million parameters and 6.2 MiB of recurrent state, whereas our target device, an Agilex 5 FPGA, has 0.87 MiB of block memory.
The state must therefore reside in external memory, and the hardware must page it in and out for every token.
Our first research question is whether this paging dominates the cost of decoding, that is, of generating one token at a time.
We answer it in hardware, for one complete layer of the model.

The model is intended for the following application, which Fig. 1 shows together with the hardware platform.
At a blind junction, a microphone array can detect an approaching vehicle before a camera sees it [3].
Our companion work, LVC-World, stores such detections in a structured description of the scene [4].
A language-model stage, which we refer to as the semantic layer, answers semantic queries about the scene, but it is much slower than the acoustic detection.
The system therefore stores the answers in a scene cache and invokes the semantic layer again only when the scene changes, which is a cache miss.
This paper presents hardware for the language model of the semantic layer.
This hardware, which we refer to as the decode tile, computes one layer of the model for one token.
We evaluated the tile and the acoustic processing of the application (the front-end) on the same FPGA, in separate bitstreams (configurations of the FPGA).

The design point is one tile that computes the recurrent layers of the model one after another.
In such a system, the weights and the recurrent state of all layers reside in external memory, so the tile reads the weights of the current layer from there and pages its state in and out.
Our experiments exercise the tile with one layer.
The closest related accelerator, in contrast, keeps a recurrent state of 2 MB on chip [5].
Two calculated numbers indicate that the state is a small part of the work of our model.
First, for an input text (prompt) of 744 tokens, the update of the recurrent state is only 2.48 % of the multiply-accumulate operations (MACs) per decoded token.
Second, the paging moves 26.0 MB per decoded token, which is 7.7 % or 11.2 % of the calculated memory traffic for the two number formats that we consider (Section 5-5.3).
For both formats, the weights are the largest part of the traffic.

Measurements on the board support this calculation.
We report the latency per layer-token, which is one token passing through one layer.
At 75 MHz and with synthetic weights, the tile takes 11.15 ms per layer-token.
The matrix-vector products with the weights take about 62 % of the cycles, the other arithmetic of the layer takes 25 %, and the state phase, which includes the paging, takes 13 %.
For this model and this memory interface, the state is therefore not the bottleneck.

Our second research question is whether the hardware computes exactly what it should.
A recurrent state carries a numerical error from one token to all later tokens, so we require bit-exact agreement between the hardware and its reference.
In this paper, bit-exact means that a hardware result equals the result of a fixed-point software reference in every bit.
We check this agreement in the simulation of the register-transfer-level (RTL) design and on the FPGA board, which the title refers to as silicon.
Section 5-5.5 also evaluates the accuracy of the fixed-point reference against 32-bit floating point (fp32).

The decode tile implements one complete recurrent layer of the model, which consists of input and output projections, a causal convolution, a gated update of the recurrent state and a gated multilayer perceptron (MLP).
Of the 24 layers of the model, 18 are of this kind.
The other six layers are attention layers, and they are outside the scope of this paper, as is the complete inference loop of the model.
The tile is one node of a mesh network-on-chip.
The other five nodes are processing elements that switch among three operating modes (tri-mode), and one request can address several nodes (multicast).
On the board, the complete layer runs with synthetic weights, which have the memory layout of the real weights and for which the simulation provides the exact expected values, and a separate test runs the update of the state with real inputs.

The paper makes three contributions.

It quantifies the cost of state paging for a complete layer, by calculation (Section 5) and by measurement on an edge FPGA (Section 8).

It integrates the tile with a mesh of tri-mode processing elements and measures the cost of a mode switch in clock cycles (Sections 4 and 8).

It presents a verification flow that measures the error of the fixed-point arithmetic against fp32 in software and checks the RTL and the board for bit-exact agreement with the fixed-point reference (Sections 5-5.5 and 8).
This flow exposed an error in a numerical limit of the RTL and several implementation faults that the original simulation tests had not detected.

title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
authors: Suvarna Kadam(Witsense AI),Soran Parsa(University of Huddersfield)
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under four years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data (π0\pi_{0}) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3–7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.
introduction:
Large language and vision-language models (VLMs) acquire broad semantic knowledge from internet-scale data. Robot learning, by contrast, has historically trained a separate policy for each robot, task and environment, using datasets several orders of magnitude smaller. Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect the two. A VLA starts from a pretrained VLM and fine-tunes it to emit actions alongside, or instead of, text. The term was introduced with RT-2 [1], which expressed robot actions as text tokens, co-fine-tuned a VLM on robot trajectories and web data, and showed emergent semantic generalisation. Since then the design space has grown at every stage of a VLA’s life cycle. In the model, action heads now range from discrete tokens to diffusion and flow matching, and pipelines from single networks to dual-system and hierarchical designs. In training, data has grown from tens of thousands of teleoperated episodes to tens of thousands of hours of multi-robot experience, supplemented by human video, simulation and the robot’s own autonomous attempts. In deployment, models that compute at a few hertz must still control robots smoothly at tens of hertz.

This survey has five aims:

A life-cycle taxonomy. We organise VLA research along seven design axes that follow a VLA’s life cycle, from model design through training to deployment (Section 3), so that a new model can be placed by the choices it makes on each; Table 3 places 22 main models this way.

Manipulation and navigation side by side. Most VLA surveys concentrate on manipulation. We treat navigation VLAs as a parallel lineage (Section 5), cover locomotion and humanoid whole-body control (Section 6), and discuss the recent convergence of manipulation and navigation (Section 7).

A data-centred quantitative view. For every work we extract the training data each paper reports and plot the field’s trajectory in robot episodes and in parameter count (Figure 6, Tables 5 and 6).

VLAs versus world-action models, and fair evaluation. We compare VLAs with world-action models (Section 8) and review standard benchmarks and the recent efforts to make VLA evaluation fair and predictive of real-world performance (Section 9).

Open problems, including a reporting problem we encountered directly: training data is described in incompatible units, or not quantified at all, in a large share of papers (Section 10).

Figure 1 places the main works on a single timeline.

We include works that condition a learned policy on vision and language and produce robot actions or action-level intermediates. Candidates were found by starting from widely used VLAs, following their references and the works that cite them, and searching arXiv; this is a structured, not a systematic, review. A work is discussed in the text if it meets at least one of three criteria:

it introduces an original idea, such as a new action representation, architecture or training signal;

it makes clear progress on a core problem (manipulation, navigation or locomotion), such as a large gain in real-robot success or a new capability;

it gives the community a tool, dataset, benchmark or method that others build on.

Ma et al. [2] gave the first taxonomy of VLAs, with three strands: building blocks, low-level controllers and high-level planners. Sapkota et al. [3] cover more than 80 models with an emphasis on applications. Zhang et al. [4] classify over 300 studies into autoregressive, diffusion, reinforcement-based and hybrid paradigms. Kawaharazuka et al. [5] take a full-stack view that includes hardware, data collection and evaluation. Cui et al. [6] survey and empirically compare dual-system architectures. More recent surveys take narrower or different cuts. Shao et al. [7] divide VLM-based manipulation VLAs into monolithic models, with single- or dual-system designs, and hierarchical models that plan through interpretable intermediates. Zhong et al. [8] organise VLAs by the kind of action token they produce, Yu et al. [9] review efficiency across models, training and data, and Xu et al. title: Heavy Metal Acrobatics: Learning Dynamic Control for Skid-Steer Loaders
authors: Pierre-Jean Lorentz,Pascal Egli,Edo Jelavic,Cliff Li,Ramitha Sundar,Harikrishnan Suresh,Paul Montgomery,Lee Redden,Matthias Müller,Ozan Sener,Vladlen Koltun,Marco Hutter
abstract:
Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous.
Here, we show that  RL (RL) in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels. This work demonstrates that RL and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors.

title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems
authors: Grid Robotics:Qingfeng Lan,Duo Li,Siyao Li,Yiheng Lyu,Shijian Lu,Zhenghao Qi,Shizun Wang,Xinchao Wang,Ming Yang,Zhiqin Yang,Zuhao Yang,Tao Yu

abstract:
The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap.
We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics.
Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences.
Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance.
Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy.
On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.
introduction:
A central goal of robotics is to enable robots to translate human intent into desired outcomes in the physical world. Early autonomous robots often integrated hand-engineered components for perception, planning, and control within modular or layered architectures (Nilsson, 1984; Gat et al., 1998).
Since then, advances in deep learning have allowed robots to learn increasingly complex behaviors.
Policies learned in simulation, mostly with deep reinforcement learning, have produced agile locomotion (Hwangbo et al., 2019) and versatile humanoid whole-body control by tracking human motion data (Liao et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026c; Liao et al., 2026).
However, these simulation-trained policies remain specialized to specific tasks and embodiments, limiting their ability to generalize across diverse and open-ended environments.
To move beyond task-specific controllers and enable robots to follow human instructions, the field has increasingly turned toward models that unify perception, language understanding, and action generation within a single framework.
Among them, vision-language-action (VLA) models, exemplified by the π\pi series, combine vision-language pretraining with diverse robot data to learn general policies that map visual observations and language instructions to actions (Black et al., 2025a; Black et al., 2025b).
More recently, world-action models (WAM) integrate video-based modeling of physical dynamics with robot policy learning (Ye et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026c). Together, these advances have broadened robot capabilities. Yet reliable generalization remains a central challenge, as policy performance can still deteriorate when scenes or instructions change (Zhou et al., 2025c).

To address this generalization challenge, a major line of research focuses on scaling and diversifying training data for VLA and WAM policies (Zheng et al., 2026; Dyna Robotics, 2026a). These efforts draw on diverse data sources, including real-robot data (Black et al., 2025a), UMI demonstrations (Chi et al., 2024), egocentric human data (Zheng et al., 2026), and multimodal web data (Brohan et al., 2023). The release of GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026b) and its early applications to robotics offered a different perspective on this challenge. In an early evaluation, the model outperformed trained policies on many robotic benchmarks without task-specific fine-tuning (Zhang et al., 2026c). Subsequent work explored its use with learned policies and robotic tools (Galbot Team et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026b). These results suggest that generalization can also be achieved by relying on a general-purpose model’s knowledge and reasoning to organize and adapt behavior during execution.
This perspective motivates a paradigm shift from policy-centric robotics to agentic robotics, by shifting the focus from learned action policies (Figure 2a) to an agent that pursues goals by coordinating skills and tools, evaluating outcomes, and adapting its decisions (Figure 2b).

Despite this progress, the community still lacks a shared understanding of agentic robotics or a reliable evaluation framework.
The scope of the paradigm, its relationship to existing forms of robot autonomy, and the organization of its constituent functions remain insufficiently clarified (Qin et al., 2026a).
Furthermore, differences in experimental conditions and system configurations also make it difficult to compare results across studies.
For example, RoboDojo evaluations of Astra vary in the task-knowledge sources they use and the action budgets they permit (Zhang et al., 2026c; SenseNova et al., 2026); separately, Harness VLA shows substantial performance gains from execution memory when the planner and VLA are held fixed (Zhang et al., 2026f).
All of these results underscore the need to establish what constitutes the agentic system, which capabilities are being assessed, and under what conditions comparisons are meaningful.
These conceptual and methodological challenges call for a unified framework that clarifies the agentic workflow by specifying the functional roles of its components and how they interact.
Such a framework can provide a shared conceptual foundation for characterizing agentic robotics, developing valid and comparable evaluations at the model and system levels, and formulating a research roadmap.

To address this, we propose a framework of agentic robotics that distinguishes three functional roles (Figure 3).
System 2 (S2) interprets intent, reasons about goals and constraints, orchestrates skills and tools, and verifies outcomes to guide subsequent decisions. System 1 (S1) provides skills and callable modules, while System 0 (S0) supplies the body interface and real-time control.
Specifically, S2 is the decision-making core of agentic robotics, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness.
The foundation model supplies knowledge, understanding, and reasoning, while the harness organizes observations, maintains plans and memory, exposes skills and tools, and supports execution and verification.
Learned policies, perception layers, motion planning modules, and generated programs are included in S1.
S2 may orchestrate these capabilities or send action targets directly to S0, while retaining responsibility for verifying outcomes and adapting its decisions.
With these roles defined, we investigate how the foundation model and harness should work together under physical constraints, and how to evaluate their contributions to closed-loop system performance.

Building on this division of responsibilities, we first explain how S2, S1, and S0 work together (Section 2).
We then articulate S2 and examine its foundation model, its harness, and the physical constraints under which they operate (Section 3).
Next, we develop an evaluation framework across nine dimensions that distinguishes model capabilities from whole system performance, and use it to assess the available evidence (Section 4).
For a closed-loop system, the framework emphasizes independent outcome verification, transparent reporting, and evaluation while the environment continues to evolve.
Furthermore, we examine which design principles carry over from digital agents to physical systems and which assumptions must be reconsidered in the physical world (Section 5).
These analyses inform a roadmap organized around four levels of delegable work, from executing primitives (L1), completing tasks (L2), coordinating workflows (L3), to fulfilling standing roles (L4) (Figure 1; Section 6).
The roadmap connects this progression to four research directions, including continual improvement from physical experience.
Finally, we conclude with several guidelines to verify and evaluate the progress of agentic robotics.

title: PROOF: Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion
authors: Siyuan Wang,Dongjie Zhu,Jinxuan Lu,Wenjun Xu,Jiankun Wang
abstract:
Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments. However, the reliability of such systems heavily depends on visual observations, which are inherently susceptible to occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination variations, often resulting in catastrophic locomotion failures under degraded perception conditions. In this paper, we present PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion), a perceptive locomotion framework that enables robust locomotion under severe visual disturbances.
Our method adopts a two-stage teacher–student learning paradigm that explicitly models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven and proprioceptive fallback behaviors, while the student predicts exteroceptive features with uncertainty and suppresses them under out-of-distribution inputs.
We evaluate our method on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a RealSense D435 depth camera in real-world settings. Under normal visual conditions, our method enables the robot to successfully perform high-dynamic parkour maneuvers, including traversing large gaps, elevated platforms, and narrow beam terrains. Under severe visual degradation, such as heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes, the robot continues to maintain stable and robust locomotion performance.
introduction:
Perceptive locomotion has significantly advanced the mobility of legged robots in complex environments [29, 17, 1]. By incorporating exteroceptive sensors such as depth cameras and LiDAR, legged robots can proactively perceive surrounding terrain geometry, enabling highly dynamic and agile behaviors including stair climbing, gap traversal, and parkour maneuvers [5, 33, 8, 21, 12, 27, 34]. Compared to traditional proprioceptive locomotion policies, perceptive locomotion provides substantially improved terrain awareness and maneuverability. However, the performance of such systems heavily depends on the reliability and accuracy of exteroceptive observations, making perception both the key enabler of agile locomotion and a major source of system vulnerability.

In real-world environments, visual perception is highly susceptible to severe environmental disturbances like sensor occlusion, illumination overexposure, reflective surfaces, motion blur and so on. Such disturbances introduce substantial out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts in visual inputs. For perceptive end-to-end locomotion policies that fully rely on exteroceptive information, corrupted visual observation directly misleads the policy’s action , ultimately resulting in unstable locomotion, collisions, or catastrophic failures.

Existing works have attempted to improve the robustness of perceptive locomotion through domain randomization, sensor dropout, adversarial perturbation training, and privileged learning mechanisms[17, 3, 24]. While these approaches improve robustness against perceptual noise and mild distribution shifts, they largely assume that exteroceptive observations remain at least partially informative. Under severe perception degradation, however, visual inputs may become fundamentally unreliable, and continuously relying on corrupted exteroceptive features can further amplify system failure. Therefore, the core challenge is not merely improving robustness to noisy perception, but enabling graceful degradation under catastrophic perception failures.

To address this challenge, we propose PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-Of-distribution Fallback), a novel two-stage perceptive locomotion framework that efficiently learns agile parkour skills while maintaining resilience against severe visual perception disturbances. To improve robustness against unreliable visual observations, we introduce a two-stage teacher–student framework with uncertainty-aware exteroceptive gating. The privileged teacher is trained with terrain elevation map under random exteroceptive masking, enabling it to learn both perception-driven agile behaviors and proprioception-based fallback locomotion. The resulting behavior is distilled into a depth-vision student, where a recurrent estimator predicts latent exteroceptive features and their uncertainty. This uncertainty serves as an input of an adaptive gate that suppresses corrupted visual inputs and falls back to proprioceptive control under OOD perception. Finally, we validate our method on a real-world Unitree Go2 equipped with a single front-facing RealSense D435 camera, demonstrating agile parkour maneuvers under clean vision and stable locomotion under severe visual degradation.

The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We present PROOF, a perceptive locomotion framework that learns agile quadruped parkour under reliable vision and falls back to proprioception when depth becomes unreliable.

We introduce a dual-guard fallback mechanism that detects OOD visual disturbances via latent uncertainty estimation and switches to proprioceptive control when vision becomes unreliable.

We validate PROOF on a real-world Unitree Go2 hardware with a single RealSense D435, showing robust obstacle traversal and failure avoidance under extreme visual corruptions.

title: Objectives as Policies: Vision-Language Model Cost Programs for Contact-Rich Manipulation
authors: Zihao Lu,Trong Gia Hung Nguyen,Fuquan Wang,Yifan Zhu
abstract:
Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong semantic and spatial reasoning capabilities in 3D environments. Recently, connecting VLMs with model-predictive controllers (MPC) has emerged as a paradigm for combining strong semantic reasoning with physics-based planning. However, connecting these two for contact-rich robotic manipulation requires a task representation that bridges the two and captures how physical interactions can be reasoned by VLMs. In this work, we
introduce Objectives as Policies (OaP), a framework that connects a
pretrained VLM to a shared sampling-based MPC through
an editable objective program. Each program specifies a sequence of stages for completing a task, combining running and terminal costs from a cost library with
stage completion conditions. Given a natural-language task instruction and scene observation, we build a simulation-based digital twin through real-to-sim, and the VLM generates an objective program that is executed by the MPC in the simulation. The program is iteratively updated by the VLM based on MPC rollouts, before being deployed in the real world. We evaluate our framework in both simulation and the real world on four tabletop manipulation tasks, and show that it outperforms strong baselines. Additional videos and examples are available on the project website: https://zihaolu001.github.io/oap-project/
introduction:
Recently, contact-implicit model-predictive control (MPC) has enabled robots to achieve real-time dexterous manipulations on various tasks [1, 2]. Compared to end-to-end learned policies, these physics-based methods naturally generalize to new objects and scenes through online re-planning and ensure safety by directly embedding safety constraints during planning. However, they require careful engineering of the rewards and constraints with the tasks and the scenes known a priori, making deployment into the open world challenging. Meanwhile, end-to-end learned policies, such as vision-language-action models, leverage the semantic understanding of vision-language models (VLMs) trained on internet-scale vision-language data and finetune with robot data to acquire robotic manipulation skills. For example, OpenVLA directly predicts actions from visual observations and language instructions, without an explicit physics model for online planning [3]. We observe that manipulation skills typically can be decomposed into two key components: what the robot should be doing, and how the robot can execute it, where the former requires semantic understanding of the environment and task, and the latter necessitates understanding of the physics and contact dynamics. Hence, in this paper, we ask the following research question: How can we integrate the semantic understanding of VLMs with physics-based MPC to achieve open-world manipulation skills, without any training data?

Previous methods have investigated the use of VLMs for robot manipulation in different ways. VoxPoser and ReKep use 3D value maps and relational keypoint constraints, respectively, for closed-loop planning [4, 5]. ReKep’s local forward model assumes grasped keypoints move rigidly with the end-effector [5], whereas our MPC explicitly simulates robot-object contact dynamics. Another method uses VLMs only for estimating the physical parameters of a world model and employs large-language models (LLMs) that script the MPC and go through iterative real-world refinement [6]. Beyond using these foundation models to generate objectives and constraints for MPCs, some works use VLMs to directly propose robot end-effector paths [7, 8]. Another class of methods trains VLMs to predict execution progress [9], which can be used as a noisy reward function during offline reinforcement learning training. Different from these methods, we propose a framework where we enhance a VLM with a digital twin obtained through real-to-sim and a library of objective terms, and allow the VLM to iteratively refine a composite objective function from simulated MPC rollouts, before real-world execution.

We introduce Objectives as Policies (OaP), a framework that expresses multi-stage tasks through an editable objective program for a shared
sampling-based MPC controller. Each program combines
running and terminal objective terms from a fixed library into a sequence of stages,
along with completion conditions for every stage. A pretrained VLM
generates the program and iteratively refines the program through rollouts in a digital twin obtained from real-to-sim, before final closed-loop execution in the real world. We leverage two refinement strategies: the first uses the VLM to self-review against the task language instruction and the scene before any rollouts, and the second updates the objective program based on the statistics of a failed rollout, which can be done iteratively over many rounds. In simulation experiments, our method achieves 90% cumulative success across four tasks with at most two feedback rounds and 97.5% with up to five rounds. title: NPU-Accelerated GNSS Signal Acquisition
authors: Taro Suzuki
abstract: On small single-board computers (SBCs), GNSS signal acquisition is a major CPU load. This paper proposes using the neural processing unit (NPU) of an SBC not for machine learning but as an accelerator for the parallel code search in GNSS signal acquisition. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) used in acquisition is decomposed by the four-step DFT into matrix products of small DFTs and expressed by 1×11\times 1 convolutions, element-wise products, and transposes, which NPUs execute efficiently. Furthermore, we propose a method that divides the DFT, the non-coherent integration, and the peak detection between the CPU and the NPU according to the configuration of the NPU (an NPU with its own memory connected via PCIe, or an NPU sharing memory with the CPU). The proposed method is implemented in the open-source software GNSS receiver Pocket SDR and evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 5 combined with the external AX8850 NPU and on the NPU built into the SoC (RK3588) of the ROCK 5C, a small SBC of comparable size. Compared with acquisition by an optimized CPU implementation, the acquisition of short codes on the Raspberry Pi 5 with the AX8850 is 3.0–3.8 times faster. In the evaluation of the whole receiver, the number of tracking channels that reach their first lock within 30 s with the NPU is 1.5 times that with the CPU, and the time until 90% of the channels are locked is reduced from 66 s to 26 s. Furthermore, because the CPU load of acquisition is reduced, the number of tracking channels that can be processed in real time increases from about 175 to about 230. These results show that using the NPU on SBCs with limited CPU resources is effective for achieving both GNSS signal acquisition and tracking. The implementation is publicly available as open source under the name PocketSDR-NPU.
introduction:
A software GNSS receiver (GNSS SDR) performs the GNSS signal processing of IF data, digitized by an RF front-end, on a general-purpose computer [27, 5]. Because the GNSS signal processing is implemented in software, new signals and algorithms can be supported easily, and GNSS SDRs are widely used in research and education. Recent open-hardware RF front-ends can simultaneously receive signals on four or more frequencies from multiple constellations. For example, Pocket SDR [35], which is published as open hardware, provides four to eight RF front-end channels for the L1, L2, L5, and L6 bands. Receiver software such as GNSS-SDR [6] and Pocket SDR is also available as open source.

There is a strong demand to run such receivers on small, low-power ARM single-board computers (SBCs) such as the Raspberry Pi. Receivers on SBCs would enable portable multi-frequency receivers and dense networks of receivers at low cost, and GNSS SDRs optimized for ARM processors have therefore been studied [36, 24]. However, the processing power of an SBC CPU is far below that of a general-purpose computer. Receiver processing consists of acquisition, which searches for the code phase and Doppler frequency of a signal, and tracking, which maintains the phase and frequency of an acquired signal. The tracking correlators impose a steady load proportional to the number of signals. In contrast, acquisition is a two-dimensional search over code phase and Doppler frequency, and a single search requires a large amount of computation even with the FFT-based parallel code search [38]. On SBCs, the acquisition load causes the following problems:

Acquisition takes a long time, which delays the initial acquisition and lengthens the time from power-on to the first fix.

Reacquisition of signals lost due to blockage is delayed, reducing the number of usable signals in real environments such as urban areas.

Acquisition occupies the CPU and limits the CPU time available for tracking. If tracking cannot keep up with real time, the whole receiver fails.

For long codes such as L1C (10 ms) and L2CM (20 ms), a direct search over the full Doppler range requires a very large amount of computation, so the direct acquisition of long codes is impractical on SBCs.

Meanwhile, NPUs for machine-learning inference have become widely available on SBCs. For example, SoCs such as the Rockchip RK3588 include a built-in NPU, and NPUs that can be connected via PCIe (M.2), such as the AX8850, are available for the widely used Raspberry Pi 5. However, an NPU is an accelerator that executes matrix products and convolutions at low precision (e.g., INT8) at high speed for the inference of machine-learning models, and it is not used for ordinary SDR signal processing.

In this paper, we therefore propose using the NPU of an SBC as a dedicated processor for GNSS signal acquisition. We build a model that expresses the DFT of the parallel code search with operations that an NPU can execute (1×11\times 1 convolution, element-wise product, and transpose), and offload the acquisition of the receiver to the NPU. The contributions of this paper are as follows:
