title: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents
authors: Yundi Cai,Zihan Wang,Chenxi Han,Yi Cheng,Houde Liu,Zilei Wang
abstract:
Independently pretrained language models and vision–language–action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM’s intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM’s subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails.
On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM–VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.
introduction:
Robotics is entering a stage in which strong general-purpose reasoning models can participate directly in the control loop. They can interpret unfamiliar instructions, identify relevant objects, reason about intermediate goals, and revise a plan after observing a failure. At the same time, VLA policies provide a powerful substrate for generating continuous robot actions from images, language, and proprioception [3, 2]. Agentic systems that combine these capabilities are a compelling route toward more general robots: a reasoning model decides what should happen next, and an action model provides the motor behavior needed to make it happen [9, 19, 7, 6].

The central challenge is making this division of labor effective. Both components may be capable in isolation, yet their composition can fail at the interface. A task-finetuned VLA may recognize a familiar scene and reproduce a familiar motion while underusing the teacher’s more specific instruction. Related work identifies visual shortcuts that allow scene information to dominate language constraints [11]. A teacher may correctly diagnose a bad approach, adjust the gripper, and restore a promising configuration, only for the student to undo that correction when control returns. These failures expose two closely related gaps: an intent gap between the teacher’s decision and the student’s behavior, and a handoff gap between the state produced by an intervention and the student’s ability to continue.

Consider an illustrative packing task. The teacher selects the red object and asks the left arm to grasp it. The student instead approaches another object, or closes its gripper before reaching a suitable contact configuration. The teacher corrects the approach and gives control back. If the student has never learned to act from this corrected state under the intended subtask, it may repeat the original motion or abandon the target. The immediate problem can be solved with more teacher control, but the same coordination failure may recur in the next episode. A system that only intervenes repeatedly spends reasoning effort without necessarily improving its underlying action capability.

Our premise is that these interactions are valuable learning data. They identify where the deployed policy diverges from a selected goal, show how that divergence can be corrected, and expose the states from which execution must resume. We therefore treat the reasoning–action interface as a target of collaborative post-training. The teacher remains an online planner, reviewer, and source of corrections. Their joint experience updates the teacher’s guidance, the shared skill vocabulary, and the student policy so that future cooperation becomes more effective. This creates a path from episodic assistance to persistent capability.

This motivates a shift from model-level to system-level post-training. In a modular embodied agent, decision guidance, the language interface, and motor behavior jointly determine what the system can accomplish. ESI makes their cooperation a learning target: interaction supplies evidence for updating each component, and their joint deployment determines the experience collected next. Through this process, the LLM’s scene understanding and corrective judgments become supervision for persistent action capability.

Web-to-robot knowledge transfer [22] and language-guided policy distillation [8] illustrate how foundation models can support embodied learning. ESI provides a pathway for converting advances in general-purpose foundation models into executable embodied capabilities. This pathway has two stages. During deployment, the LLM contributes scene understanding, planning, and corrective decisions to the current agent. Through the flywheel, effective interaction becomes supervision that updates the action policy and guidance for subsequent rounds. A foundation model thus participates both in performing tasks and in producing the experience from which the embodied system learns.

We instantiate this idea in ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), a configure-once flywheel built on the open-source GPT-as-Policy system [6] (Figure 1). During collection, the teacher selects a structured subtask, the VLA proposes an action chunk, and the teacher accepts useful motion or applies a correction. The resulting observations, instructions, reasoning, executed actions, and feedback support round-level updates of decision guidance, the shared skill catalog, and policy parameters. These components are deployed together in the next round, while the LLM’s weights remain fixed.

The link from interaction to policy improvement is the selection of locally effective behavior. ESI retains successful subtasks from unsuccessful episodes and connects teacher corrections with valid student continuations on the executed timeline. Training under the corresponding local intent teaches the policy both what operation to perform and how to continue from states reached during collaboration. Episode-level review complements this action supervision by refining the teacher’s guidance and consolidating recurring custom operations into reusable skills.

On the selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI scores higher than both individual component references on all ten tasks and exceeds both in success rate on nine. For packing objects into a box, ESI completes ten of twenty cases, against reported success rates of 0% for GPT-6-Astra and 2.67% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Section 6 reports the full comparison.

This report develops three main contributions:

System-level post-training for modular embodied agents. We make the cooperation between independently pretrained reasoning and action models a target of adaptation, updating decision guidance, the shared skill interface, and motor execution through environmental interaction.

Interaction-grounded embodied distillation. We connect semantic intent and corrective behavior to VLA learning through a shared control and supervision interface. The pipeline retains successful student behavior, effective corrections, and their continuations, including useful subtasks from unsuccessful episodes.

A framework for automated embodied self-improvement. We automate experience-driven updates of decision prompts, a shared skill catalog, and VLA parameters, and return the updated components to the next deployment round.

2. Interaction-grounded embodied distillation. We connect semantic intent and corrective behavior to VLA learning through a shared control and supervision interface. The pipeline retains successful student behavior, effective corrections, and their continuations, including useful subtasks from unsuccessful episodes.

3. A framework for automated embodied self-improvement. We automate experience-driven updates of decision prompts, a shared skill catalog, and VLA parameters, and return the updated components to the next deployment round.

title: Evaluating Language Models as Spatial Priors for Object-Goal Navigation
authors: Jun Miura
abstract: Semantic exploration methods for object-goal navigation use large language models (LLMs) to score how strongly a target object is associated with a room type or with a nearby object. This paper considers obtaining from the LLM a spatial prior instead: a distribution over the position of the target in a room. We evaluate whether two open-weight LLMs, Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, can provide such a prior. Using real room layouts from CubiCasa5K and ScanNet, we measure two outputs of the models: the likelihood they assign to real and perturbed layouts, and the layouts they generate. The object frequencies and room sizes of the generated rooms follow the room type, as in real rooms, but the proximity of the objects to the walls does not follow the differences between room types found in real rooms. The likelihood distinguishes real layouts from perturbed ones partly through their geometry and partly through the agreement between the coordinates and a field that states the wall each object touches; for the movable furniture of ScanNet, it is higher for layouts with all objects piled near the room center than for the real layouts in most rooms. When an object is given in the prompt, the models place an object related to it relative to it and move other objects away from it. When the wall of each object is given in the prompt, the models place most objects against that wall, but they do not keep all objects inside a given room rectangle. As a prior for object search, the generated placements reduce the searched area relative to a uniform prior, but by less than a third of the reduction obtained with a prior built from real layouts; when both priors are spatially smoothed, the fraction remains below two thirds, and the real-layout prior gives the lower search cost in every room type. These results support the use of LLMs for object–room associations and for writing coordinates under constraints determined by another component, followed by a geometric check, but not as a source of placement priors where real layouts are available.
introduction:
Object-goal navigation is a fundamental task for mobile service
robots. Semantic exploration is a strategy for object-goal navigation
and sometimes utilizes large language models (LLMs) for selecting next
viewpoints. Systems such as ESC, L3MVN and their successors query the
model for a scalar affinity, which indicates how strongly a
target category is associated with a room type or a nearby object, and
use it to rank frontiers
(Zhou et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2024; Jia and Yu, 2026). The model
supplies a number per candidate frontier, and the geometry is obtained
from a separate mapping process.

In this paper, we investigate whether LLMs can provide a placement rather than an affinity. If the layouts generated by a model gave the usual positions of objects in a room type, a robot could enter an unmapped room with a spatial prior over the position of the target instead of a ranking of frontiers. Language-driven scene generation systems use LLMs to generate metric layouts that look plausible
(Feng et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Çelen et al., 2024).
Their evaluations, however, measure the plausibility of the generated scenes or their agreement with the prompt; they do not compare the distribution of generated layouts with that of real rooms, which is the property that a spatial prior requires.

We evaluate the placement information that two open-weight LLMs, Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it (Qwen and Gemma below), provide along two axes: agreement with reality and usefulness for navigation. Fig. 1 shows the overview of the evaluation. We use two outputs of the models, both on real rooms from two datasets, ScanNet and CubiCasa5K. The first output is the likelihood that a model assigns to a layout written as text (Fig. 1(a)). We compare the likelihood of each real layout with that of perturbed copies, in which objects are moved, exchanged or piled up, and measure the fraction of rooms in which the real layout scores higher. The second output is the set of layouts that a model generates for a given room type (Fig. 1(b)). We compare their object frequencies, room sizes and wall proximity with those of real rooms of the same type, and examine whether a generated object moves with an object stated in the prompt. These two comparisons measure the agreement with reality. For the usefulness for navigation, we build from the generated layouts a prior over the position of a target object (Fig. 1(c)), and compute the fraction of the area of a real room that a search guided by the prior examines before it finds the target, compared with a uniform prior and with a prior built from real layouts.

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

We propose a method for evaluating LLMs as spatial priors. The method uses two outputs of the models, the likelihood of real and perturbed layouts and the generated layouts, on real rooms from two datasets, and controls for the properties of the serialized text that affect the likelihood (Secs. 3, 4 and 8.3).

We show that object frequencies and room sizes in the generated rooms follow the room type but object placement does not. We also show that the generated coordinates reflect regularities in how coordinates are written rather than the geometric constraints that determine them (Secs. 5 and 6).

We show that, when an observed object is given in the prompt, the models place a related object relative to it and move unrelated objects away from it (Sec. 5.3).

We evaluate the generated placements as a prior for object search and show that they reduce the search cost relative to a uniform prior by 0.036–0.077 of the room area for Qwen and 0.015–0.069 for Gemma, which is 14–32% and 10–23%, respectively, of the reduction obtained with a prior built from real layouts (29–48% and 30–58% when each prior is spatially smoothed). Based on all the results, we derive design guidelines for using LLMs in object-goal navigation (Secs. 7 and 8).

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Sec. 2 surveys related work. Sec. 3 describes the datasets, the serialization, the placement statistic and the generation conditions. Sec. 4 measures whether the likelihood of a real layout is higher than that of a perturbed copy, separates the effects of the geometry and of the text, and measures whether the likelihood changes when the neighbor of an object is changed. Sec. 5 measures which properties of generated layouts depend on the room type, and whether placement follows an object stated in the prompt. Sec. 6 analyzes the generated coordinates. Sec. 7 evaluates the generated placements as a search prior. Sec. 8 states the design guidelines, Sec. 9 the limitations, and Sec. 10 concludes. Appendix A defines every quantity, Appendix B reproduces the prompts, and Appendix C the output schemas. The tables of Appendix A give every number the main text summarizes, each placed after the definition it depends on.

title: PoliMop: Policy-in-the-Loop Motion Planning in 3D Spaces for Mobile Robots
authors: Yael Fassbind,Valentin N. Hartmann,Huang Su,Yijiang Huang,Stelian Coros
abstract:
Reaching a goal state in a complex environment often requires a robot to overcome challenging terrain and obstacles.
Which routes are accessible depends on the robot’s physical design, the control policy it uses, and how it modifies its surroundings.
We present a kinodynamic rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) planner that uses physics simulation to exploit skills encoded in the control policy, which allows it to find a path in the scene with respect to the robot’s capabilities.
The planner samples states from a reduced state space in 3D around the scene and expands the RRT toward each sample using policy rollouts.

introduction:
Motion planning is typically treated as the problem of finding a feasible path through a fixed environment.
For robots operating in complex terrain, however, reachability depends not only on the scene geometry but also on the robot’s body and brain, i.e., its mechanical design and control policies.
A path that is feasible for a quadruped equipped with a parkour control policy (e.g., [1]) may be infeasible for a wheeled robot or for the same quadruped using a simpler locomotion policy.
Moreover, a robot can intentionally change the scene by manipulating objects to actively extend its reachable space.
For example, a robot may place a plank across a gap to create a bridge to make a final platform reachable.
Thus, reachability is not a fixed property of the scene: it emerges from the combination of the robot, the selected policy, and the current environment state.
Ultimately, our vision is to enable robots not only to exploit the capabilities of their control policies to traverse challenging terrain but also to deliberately modify their environment to reach a goal or complete a task.
In this work, we take a step toward this goal by asking: how can a motion planner find paths in environments whose reachable regions change through prescribed manipulation actions and policy selections?

Many conventional motion-planning approaches use explicit representations of traversable terrain, such as 2.5D elevation maps combined with robot-specific traversability estimates [2, 3].
A single-layer elevation map stores one terrain height per horizontal location and therefore cannot perform motion planning on vertically overlapping surfaces (Fig. 1, right).
Additionally, the planner should automatically exploit the robot’s capabilities encoded in its control policy.
To achieve both, our planner samples target positions throughout the 3D scene and uses a physics simulator as a state-transition mechanism to roll out motions generated by the control policy.
This enables us to plan through multi-level structures, as illustrated in Fig. 1, while accounting for the selected robot–policy pair’s capabilities without the requirement of an explicit parameterization of the reachable space that the planner needs to sample from.

We formulate our approach in the framework of kinodynamic RRT [4, 5] as its incremental tree structure provides a natural way to explore an environment through policy-driven rollouts.
During each expansion, we use a policy rollout to produce a motion such that the robot moves toward a sampled target in 3D.
Therefore, the RRT explores the reachable space produced by the selected robot–policy pair, allowing capabilities such as walking up stairs (Fig. 1) or even climbing walls to emerge without being modeled explicitly.
This also means that our planner can adapt to new robot models, control policies, or 3D scene changes in a plug-and-play manner, without needing to change the motion-planning framework.

Our contributions include:

A policy-in-the-loop kinodynamic Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) that uses a physics simulator to evaluate control-policy rollouts, such that exploration reflects the capabilities of the selected robot–policy pair in the current environment.

A path-guided sampling strategy that reduces planning time by focusing on promising regions of the state space using a simplified mass-point model.

title: A Generalizable Approach to Safety-Aware Robotic Behavior Planning with an Explicit Constraint Space
authors: Xianxu Wu,Shang-Ching Liu,Zhaocong Liang,Hengxiang Chen,Yujian Ma,Shenwen Deng,Qiang Li,Jianwei Zhang
abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation, context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.
introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have significantly advanced robotic behavior planning by enabling robots to interpret natural-language instructions, understand visual scenes, and generate long-horizon action sequences [1, 2, 3]. However, completing a task does not necessarily imply completing it safely. In tabletop manipulation, the same instruction may involve different safety requirements depending on the surrounding environment. For example, manipulating a liquid near electronic devices or operating a sharp object near a human requires safety considerations that may not be explicitly stated in the task instruction. Therefore, a safety-aware robot must not only understand what task to perform, but also identify the safety constraints imposed by the current task and environment [4].

To make such safety knowledge explicit and reusable, we maintain a Constraint Space consisting of textual safety rules. This representation separates safety knowledge from the planner itself and allows the same constraints to be reused across different tasks and scenes. However, maintaining a rule library introduces another challenge: only a small subset of constraints is typically applicable to a particular task and environment. Selecting rules merely according to semantic similarity does not necessarily reflect whether a constraint should actually be enforced in the current scene. The key problem is therefore to determine the applicability of each constraint conditioned jointly on the task and the environment.

We address this problem with a lightweight query-conditioned constraint applicability model. Given a natural-language task and a visual observation, the environment is first represented in textual form and combined with the task to form a contextual query. A dual-tower model then evaluates the constraints in the Constraint Space and selects an applicable subset, which is provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. In this way, safety constraints are explicitly selected before planning rather than being left entirely to the implicit safety reasoning of the planner.

A fixed Constraint Space and a fixed applicability model, however, cannot cover every safety situation encountered at test time. The selected constraint set may contain irrelevant rules, omit safety-critical ones, or fail to represent a previously unseen hazard. We therefore introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that examines the generated primitive plan and, when necessary, jointly produces a corrected plan proposal and reconstructs the complete set of constraints applicable to the current task and environment. The reconstructed constraints are returned to the planner for corrective re-planning. After validation by a post-reviewer, Inspector-generated feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of both the constraint-applicability model and the Safety Inspector, with the latter adapted through LoRA. Newly identified constraints are also incorporated into the Constraint Space. In this way, the framework can continuously improve constraint selection, safety inspection, and the explicit safety knowledge available for future planning.

Our contributions are threefold:

Query-Conditioned Constraint Applicability Learning.
We formulate safety-constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning and introduce a lightweight dual-tower model in which each contextual query induces a separating boundary over learned constraint representations.

Multimodal Safety Inspection with Constraint Reconstruction.
We introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that goes beyond binary safety verification by jointly producing a corrected primitive-plan proposal and reconstructing the complete set of constraints applicable to the current task and environment.

Inspector-Guided Test-Time Adaptation and Knowledge Expansion.
We use validated Inspector feedback to adapt both the lightweight constraint-applicability model and the Safety Inspector through parameter-efficient LoRA updates, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space for explicit safety-knowledge expansion.

We introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that goes beyond binary safety verification by jointly producing a corrected primitive-plan proposal and reconstructing the complete set of constraints applicable to the current task and environment.

title: Reusing Locomotion Training Recipes Across Humanoids via Body-Aligned Virtual Joints
authors: Sol Choi,Mingon Kim,Seokin Seo,Jongeun Choi,Donghyeon Kim,Yisoo Lee
abstract:
Reinforcement learning has enabled robust humanoid locomotion, yet training
recipes—rewards, architectures, hyperparameters—remain hard to reuse
across robots with different native joint coordinates, since policies
output native joint angles while action scales, bounds, gains, and
penalties are defined in those robot-specific coordinates. Existing
transmission models convert native targets into actuator commands but do
not standardize the coordinate interface exposed to the policy. We
introduce a body-aligned virtual joint space upstream of this
mapping: policy actions and observations follow a common anatomical
convention, and a deterministic kinematic layer maps virtual targets to
native ones, leaving the existing transmission and low-level control stack
unchanged. Under a single unmodified recipe on three humanoids with
different leg-axis layouts, it is the only interface that tracks
accurately, keeps the feet aligned with the travel direction, and trains
stably on all three, and on Unitree G1 hardware it reduces heading drift
by nearly a factor of six.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled legged robots to acquire dynamic behaviors that transfer from simulation to hardware. Learned controllers have demonstrated agile quadrupedal locomotion [1, 2], traversal over challenging terrain [3, 4], rapid adaptation to changing dynamics [5], and training within minutes using massively parallel simulation [6]. Similar techniques have produced dynamic bipedal walking [7], stair traversal [8], and real-world humanoid locomotion [9, 10]. Nevertheless, adapting a controller to a robot with a different joint layout often requires substantial retraining and retuning by different training recipes.

As seen in Fig. 1, such kinematic diversity is often a deliberate consequence of mechanical design rather than an arbitrary modeling choice. Humanoid legs must generate large torques within tightly constrained volumes while keeping distal mass and inertia low. Designers therefore relocate actuators away
from joint centers, employ linkage or parallel transmissions to obtain favorable leverage and distribute loads across actuators, and incline joint axes to improve workspace or locomotion-specific force transmission  [11, 12, 13].
These choices can improve torque density and dynamic performance, but they also produce oblique, coupled, or configuration-dependent joint coordinates instead of a uniform body-aligned orthogonal arrangement.

In this study, we focus on the hypothesis that part of this embodiment dependence originates from the coordinates in which policy actions are expressed. Most locomotion policies output desired angles in the robot’s native joint space [2, 6, 7, 9]. Consider a body-aligned hip-roll motion. If the hip axes are aligned with the pelvis frame, the motion may correspond mainly to one native joint. With oblique axes, the same motion requires coordinated changes of several native joints, even when they are independently actuated. Such axes may be introduced for packaging, range-of-motion, and mechanical-design considerations [13]. The same task-level motion can therefore acquire a different numerical representation on each robot.

This issue is distinct from the conventional joint-to-actuator mapping. Four-bar linkages, parallel ankles, and other closed-chain transmissions are commonly handled by converting generalized joint targets into actuator commands [11, 12, 14]. These models describe how a robot-native joint motion is physically realized, but do not make the native coordinates themselves consistent across robots. Our method adds a virtual-to-native coordinate layer upstream of, rather than replacing, the existing transmission layer.

A sufficiently expressive policy can learn this relation implicitly, but then known embodiment-specific kinematics becomes embedded in the controller. A fixed orthogonal change of basis does not reduce the coverage of isotropic exploration. Practical locomotion pipelines, however, are not fully coordinate invariant: they commonly use factorized action distributions and per-joint scaling, clipping, gains, limits, and regularization [7, 10, 15]. Changing the native coordinates thus changes the correlations, relative scales, saturation margins, and penalties associated with an equivalent body-level motion.

Prior work has shown that action representation affects locomotion learning. Reference-relative joint targets provide useful structure [16], task-space actions can improve learning efficiency [17], and torque actions exhibit different tuning and transfer characteristics from position targets [18]. Cross-embodiment methods instead seek generalization through graph-structured or modular policies [19, 20], morphology-conditioned architectures [21, 22, 23], and multi-embodiment training [24]. These approaches are complementary to ours: we standardize the physical meaning of the joint-level action before robot-specific coordinate and transmission mappings are applied.

The contributions are threefold: (i) we identify native-coordinate inconsistency—distinct from the joint-to-actuator transmission, which existing models already handle—as a source of embodiment dependence, and address it with an analytic coordinate layer derived from the kinematic model that maps actions, joint-velocity observations, and joint-space gains
between a shared body-aligned space and each robot’s native space; (ii) we show that where the map is inserted during training matters: applying it post-hoc avoids an instability that arises when it is composed in the training loop; and (iii) we evaluate the interface on three humanoids and on Unitree G1 hardware, where the benefit appears first in gait geometry rather than in aggregate task error.

title: Per-Agent-Safe Navigation of Globally Driven Robot Collectives via Affine Field Design
authors: Seunghwan Jang,Steven Ceron,Wei Xiao
abstract:
Safe navigation of robot collectives requires coordinating motion and deformation so that the collective can traverse constrained environments while ensuring each robot’s safety.
Existing controllers for swarmalator collectives largely rely on local control, where each robot receives an individual command, which causes the control and communication requirements to grow with the number of agents.
We introduce a broadcast control formulation in which a single spatially affine field governs both the motion and deformation of the collective.
The scalar component of the field regulates collective size, and its spatial gradient generates collective translation through non-reciprocal interactions.
Both components enter the collective dynamics directly, which allows per-robot wall, actuation, and cohesion constraints to be enforced using control barrier functions within a single quadratic program for the whole collective.
The resulting controller continuously adapts the collective size to the local environment, and enables safe passage through corridors narrower than the unconstrained collective without pre-planned resizing.
We further derive how the available actuation budget determines the reachable speed and minimum passable corridor width, and we demonstrate that two independently driven collectives can simultaneously traverse a shared junction using distinct fixed phase labels without inter-collective coordination.
introduction:
Robot collective is becoming increasingly popular as it can efficiently manage the behaviors of a large set of robot agents while performing complex tasks.
The simplest way to control a robot collective is to send the same global signal to every robot, and for sufficiently small robots this is often the only practical option
[1, 2, 3] as they may not have local computation capability.
Broadcast control considers the setting where a large population of simple robots responds to a shared input and individual robots cannot receive separate commands [4].
The challenge is that all of the collective behaviors, including safe navigation, must then arise from this single input.
This differs from many swarm robotics studies, where
individual robots typically execute their own programs or receive their own control commands [5, 6].

The swarmalator model [7] offers a natural framework for controlling such collectives.
Originally introduced to describe agents that simultaneously swarm in space and synchronize an internal phase, the model can generate a wide range of collective behaviors using only a small number of global coupling parameters [8, 9, 10]. These behaviors have been realized on physical robots
[11, 12] and have also been shown to capture the self-organization of microrobot collectives [2].
More recent work has used the swarmalator model as a framework for controlling robot collectives. Non-reciprocal coupling, in which the influence of one agent on another is not necessarily equal and opposite, can generate controllable collective locomotion and formations [13, 14], while control barrier functions (CBFs) can be used to safely navigate these collectives through obstacle-laden environments [15, 16].

Existing collective controllers, however, still depend on local control, where each robot receives its own command; for example, in [13] and [14] each agent receives its own coupling parameter, and in the local mode of [15] its own velocity command.
The one variant that operates under a single shared input adds a common velocity to every robot, so that the collective can only translate as a rigid body, and, as its authors report, the fixed safety margin around the formation then prevents it from passing through narrow corridors [15].
This limitation is not specific to one controller but follows from how the coupling has been used.
Under a shared input, prior work has regulated size through the phase coupling rather than the spatial coupling; the phase coupling enters the phase dynamics but not the position dynamics, so a barrier condition written on robot positions cannot act on phase directly, and in practice the collective is resized outside the control loop by a pre-planned transition [16].
However, a pre-planned resizing cannot respond to geometry that the plan did not anticipate due to uncertainties.
The alternative of placing the size parameter in a higher-order barrier [13, 17] brings size back into the loop, but only at the cost of an additional integral control input.

In this paper we propose a broadcast formulation in which a single input produces motion, deformation, and safety within one optimization, by designing the input as a spatially affine field over the collective.
Each robot experiences this field at its own position, so a single control input yields a different coupling for each robot.
The scalar term in the affine field raises or lowers all couplings together and thereby sets the size of the collective, while the gradient term creates a coupling difference across the collective and, through the non-reciprocity of the interaction, drives it forward.
Both terms act on the centroid and the second moment of the collective with relative degree one, so a wall constraint written for each robot at its own position and a size bound derived from the local geometry enter a
single quadratic program (QP) as hard constraints.
The collective then compresses at every control step as a corridor narrows, without any schedule.
Beyond a single collective, assigning each collective a distinct phase label admits several of them to share a space without any inter-collective coordination.

Our contributions are as follows: (1) we formulate broadcast control of a swarmalator collective in which the control input is a spatially affine field and safety, actuation, and cohesion constraints are imposed for every agent on a single broadcast whose size does not depend on the number of agents; (2) we show that under this formulation the position and the size of the collective can both be automatically constrained by standard CBFs, so that safety and size regulation are handled in one optimization and the collective passes corridors that translation alone cannot; (3) we derive the reachable speed and the minimum passable width from a single actuation budget and verify the predicted minimum width in simulation; and (4) we show that several collectives can be operated without coordination by assigning each a distinct phase label, demonstrate two collectives crossing a junction simultaneously, and derive a bound on the number of collectives that phase labels alone can keep apart.

introduction:
For a domestic service robot to provide continuous and personalized services in homes, offices, or care facilities, it must identify users and respond to each of them individually.
For example, guiding a person or fetching an object based on a previous conversation is only possible when the robot can recognize who it is interacting with.
Therefore, person identification is an important capability for service robots that are expected to provide assistance based on users’ preferences and previous interactions.

In real-world environments, however, person identification is challenging
because only a small number of observations may be available for learning.
At the same time, observation conditions can change substantially between
learning and identification.
For example, visual appearance may change because of clothing, posture,
or worn items; speech signals may be degraded by household and ambient
noise; and utterance content may vary between encounters.
As a result, a robot must identify users robustly from limited training
observations even when multiple modalities change simultaneously.

To address this challenge, we propose a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of visual, acoustic, and linguistic observations.
An overview of this study is shown in Fig. 1.
First, the robot collects visual, acoustic, and linguistic observations
of users in the environment. Next, visual and linguistic features are extracted using Contrastive
Language-Image Pre-training

(CLIP) [1], while acoustic features
are extracted using Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining
(CLAP) [2], and these features are compressed using principal
component analysis (PCA).
The extracted multimodal features are then integrated by the
nonparametric Bayesian model based on the Chinese restaurant process
(CRP) [3] to form person concepts.

Because the number of concepts is inferred from the observations rather
than specified in advance, the model can learn person concepts without
using person labels or prior knowledge of the number of users.
Finally, when a new observation is obtained, the model compares it with
the learned person concepts and identifies the person based on the

title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
authors: Yu Zhou,Changsong Lei,Yixiang Wei,Kairui Wen,Huankun Sheng,Ming Li,Yeying Fan,Yu-Hui Wen,Yong-Jin Liu
abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices—reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance—cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.
introduction:
World models intended for planning and control need to capture how an agent’s actions affect future states [37, 17]. However, the large-scale video data used to train such models rarely include synchronized low-level action annotations, while robot trajectories with such labels are costly to collect and limited in task and embodiment coverage [44, 5, 49]. This mismatch poses a central challenge for embodied learning: a world model can make future predictions, whereas planning and control require a representation of how an agent’s actions change the future.

Latent-action models seek to bridge this gap by inferring compact action-like variables from consecutive observations, thereby enabling action-conditioned learning from unlabeled video [44, 5, 49]. These inferred variables are treated as latent actions and are intended to serve as proxies for the unobserved physical actions that connect successive observations. Existing evaluations of latent-action models, however, raise a basic question [45]: when a latent improves prediction, does it contribute action-related information, or does it merely preserve predictive structure already present in the logged trajectory?

Distinguishing action-related information from predictable trajectory structure is especially challenging in offline robot datasets, where the current state alone may strongly constrain the demonstrator’s next action. For instance, Figure 1(a) shows a trajectory from the ALOHA static-battery release in which the grippers and manipulated material are already in contact [51]. The frame therefore reveals both the contact state and the task phase, making the subsequent motion more predictable even without a latent action. A latent that preserves these state cues may improve future prediction without contributing additional action-related information beyond the current state. More generally, the scene and episode cues visible in Figure 1(b) may help predict typical transitions without representing the agent’s action, and episode progress and temporal regularities can provide similar non-action shortcuts [11, 33].

A second confound arises from the evaluation model itself. A predictor that receives both the current state and a latent may have greater effective capacity than a predictor that receives the state alone, so a lower prediction loss need not reflect action-related information in the latent [21]. Consequently, transition-prediction loss, reconstruction quality, action-prediction accuracy, and downstream policy success cannot, in isolation, determine whether improved performance reflects action-related information rather than state predictability, non-action shortcuts, or differences in evaluation capacity.

Table 1 shows that prior work evaluates latent-action models using heterogeneous outcomes, including policy success, latent-action correlation, reconstruction fidelity, and planning performance. Because these quantities measure different objects on different scales, their values do not define a common measure of latent quality. We therefore formulate latent-action evaluation as a metric-design problem: an evaluation metric must first specify what it means for a learned latent to function as an action. We adopt a functional definition in which a learned latent functions as an action to the extent that it contributes action-related information about an evaluation target beyond what is available from the current state and from plausible non-action shortcuts. We call this property latent action support. We use the recorded physical action and one-step physical state change as targets, and compare the latent with the current state and non-action variables such as episode progress and episode identity.

We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric for measuring whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond what the current state and a plausible non-action control can explain. A lower LASR score indicates stronger support, with one serving as the operational boundary. Across targets and data splits, LASR offers two complementary summaries: GeoLASR summarizes typical support, whereas WorstLASR exposes the weakest case. Known action and non-action examples check whether the metric behaves as intended, while our analysis explains why the comparison captures information contributed by the latent.

Building on the LASR metric, we also construct the LASR benchmark, which provides a common setting for applying LASR to different representations. We further use LASR’s relative comparison to train a small residual adapter and test whether it makes action-related information in a frozen latent easier to use. We compare the adapted representation with the original latent and several compression and training alternatives, and use paired uncertainty to assess the reliability of the differences. Additional matched multi-task, probe/control, physical-replay, and intervention audits test whether the main interpretation survives broader confounds without changing the metric definition.

We make the following three contributions:

We introduce LASR, a dimensionless metric for quantifying latent action support. Building on LASR, we define GeoLASR and WorstLASR as complementary aggregate summaries of typical and worst-case support, respectively, and construct the LASR benchmark for consistent comparisons across representations.

We provide a theoretical characterization of latent-action information through a conditional Bayes-risk identity, oracle retention, and an information boundary for deterministic post-hoc adapters.

Experiments on robot manipulation data show that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and supports graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. Matched multi-task and intervention audits broaden this validation, while a lightweight residual adapter illustrates a secondary use of the LASR-inspired surrogate under paired uncertainty.

title: When Does Cross-View Consistency Matter in Multi-View Appearance Augmentation? A Controlled Study for Visuomotor Policies
authors: Zixuan Jiang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Multi-view visual augmentation often seeks consistency across cameras, but it is unclear which forms of consistency matter for downstream control. We use simulation-state replay to manipulate cross-view coupling while preserving the per-camera perturbation distributions, physical trajectories, and action labels. Across seven LIBERO manipulation tasks, marginal-matched changes in global appearance, ghost injection, and target color have small average costs for a late-fusion Diffusion Policy: point estimates are near zero or negative, and the largest upper endpoint of the 90% posterior credible intervals is 2.55 percentage points. In contrast, geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations (90% CrI [0.64, 6.28]), with displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and the number of affected views matched. Camera interventions reveal substantial dependence on wrist-view geometry, while feature analysis shows appearance sensitivity patterns associated with the factors randomized during training. ACT shows a higher target-color cost estimate than DP, with uncertainty that includes zero and sensitivity to task composition. Within the tested tasks and policy configurations, these findings motivate selective consistency constraints: appearance coupling can sometimes be relaxed, whereas task-relevant geometry and cross-view spatial correspondence warrant protection.
introduction:
Generative visual augmentation can change the backgrounds, lighting, and object appearances in recorded robot demonstrations while reusing their action labels [1, 2, 3]. This offers a route to broader visual coverage without collecting new physical trajectories. For policies that observe both a third-person camera and a wrist camera, however, augmentation must also decide how the generated views relate to one another. Independently editing each camera is straightforward but may yield incompatible observations; generating views jointly can enforce consistency but adds modeling and computational requirements.

Does stronger cross-view consistency necessarily improve downstream control? A direct comparison between independent and joint generators does not isolate this question. Such generators can differ simultaneously in single-view quality, visual diversity, and cross-view coupling. Moreover, “inconsistency” is not a single intervention. Conflicting background textures, different target colors, and contradictory target positions need not have the same consequences for action selection.

We study the control value of coupling with a controlled simulation design. Recorded LIBERO states are replayed and rendered separately for each camera. We construct joint perturbation distributions with the same per-camera marginals, so that a camera receives the same distribution of perturbations regardless of how its perturbation is paired with the other view. This yields an estimate of the net control effect of changing cross-view coupling, at a fixed distribution of perturbations for each camera.

Our main experiments use a late-fusion Diffusion Policy (DP) on seven manipulation tasks. Marginal-matched global-appearance, ghost, and target-color contrasts have small average costs. At the same time, masking the wrist camera or introducing an unseen target displacement substantially reduces success. A further experiment matches the displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and number of affected cameras, and finds that geometrically anti-coupled observations are worse than coupled observations. Feature and co-visibility measurements provide descriptive context, and ACT supplies an exploratory comparison of policy configurations.

The contributions are threefold: (1) a state-replay design that manipulates cross-view joint distributions while preserving per-camera perturbation marginals; (2) downstream control estimates for several appearance contrasts and a marginal-matched geometry contrast; and (3) camera interventions and descriptive measurements that delineate the scope of the behavioral findings. Together, these contributions motivate allocating consistency constraints according to the visual information needed for control.

title: ERA: Error-Resistant Autonomous Object Navigation with Predicted Depth
authors: Shunyang Huang,Shuo Wang,Wenyuan Xie,Mingyu Lin,Yue Ding,Hongtao Lu
abstract:
Depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry from RGB images, allowing zero-shot object navigation without a depth sensor.
However, when predicted depth is mapped as if it came from a sensor, view-dependent errors accumulate in the map, remove exploration goals, and end the search before the agent can observe and correct them.
We propose ERA, a training-free object navigation system that replaces the depth sensor with depth predicted from RGB images and poses.
ERA follows a paradigm we call Move with Error: movement provides new views that correct map errors, and the corrected map enables further movement.
It realizes this paradigm with revisable occupancy and with exploration from reachable viewpoints, which continues the search when no frontier remains, and verifies the target across views before stopping.
On three benchmarks, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors.
Its map and exploration components also raise VLFM’s success from 10.8%10.8\% to 61.7%61.7\% under the same predicted depth.
We further deploy ERA on a real robot.
introduction:
Zero-shot object navigation combines the semantic knowledge of foundation models with geometric maps to find objects in unseen environments [37, 35, 36, 40]. These maps guide where to move, what to explore, and when to stop. Most map-based systems rely on depth sensors for geometry, but recent depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry directly from RGB observations [13, 26], enabling navigation without dedicated depth sensing. Existing RGB-only methods either reason in image space [3, 10, 30] or reconstruct geometry before planning [39, 31]. This raises a central question: how should an agent navigate when the geometry on which it acts is inevitably imperfect?

Replacing sensor depth with predicted depth can cause premature termination.
On HM3D v2, this substitution reduces VLFM’s [37] success rate from 68.2%68.2\% to 10.8%10.8\%, despite a mean relative depth error of about 10%10\% (a); L3MVN [38], which uses a different map and planner, also degrades substantially. Our analysis in Sec. 2 reveals how this failure arises: inconsistent predictions of the same surface accumulate into thicker obstacles, closing passages and eliminating frontiers—the boundaries between observed free space and unknown space (b–d). Consequently, VLFM stops when no frontier remains, while L3MVN often stops when no exploration goal has an executable path. Once exploration stops, the agent can no longer acquire observations that might correct the map, leaving the errors that caused termination uncorrected.

This failure exposes a circular dependency: correcting the map requires new viewpoints, yet reaching those viewpoints is itself governed by the map.
We break this dependency with the Move with Error paradigm: an agent should not treat the map only as a basis for navigation, but also use movement to acquire new observations that can test and revise its geometric understanding.
This paradigm requires two coupled capabilities. First, observations acquired through movement must be able to correct earlier geometric estimates when new viewpoints reveal contradictory evidence (Move2Error). Second, the agent must continue seeking reachable viewpoints even when accumulated map errors eliminate its conventional exploration goals (Error2Move).
Neither capability is sufficient on its own: map revision cannot help if the agent can no longer reach new viewpoints, while continued movement cannot correct the map if subsequent observations cannot revise earlier estimates.
Together, they establish a mutually reinforcing feedback loop in which movement enables map correction, and map correction enables further movement.

We instantiate Move with Error in ERA, a training-free zero-shot object navigation system that uses RGB observations and pose estimates.
Revisable occupancy lets later free-space observations remove erroneous obstacles while retaining geometry that no new evidence contradicts (Move2Error).
Exploration from reachable viewpoints selects goals throughout reachable known-free space instead of only at frontiers, so that the agent keeps acquiring new views when no frontier remains (Error2Move).
The two mechanisms close the loop: exploration provides the observations needed for correction, and revisable occupancy turns them into map updates that reopen routes for further exploration.
ERA further uses target verification, which updates candidate geometry during approach and requires agreement across views before stopping.

By improving its resistance to errors during autonomous navigation, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors on three benchmarks.
The two mechanisms also transfer to existing systems: added to VLFM, they raise its success under the same predicted depth from 10.8%10.8\% to 61.7%61.7\% (e) without changing its perception or controller; experiments with L3MVN and a second depth model further support their generality.
We also deploy ERA on a real robot using a single RGB camera and wheel odometry to validate its effectiveness and robustness.

Our contributions are threefold:

We analyze how predicted-depth errors propagate through mapping and exploration, revealing a failure in which geometric errors eliminate exploration goals and prevent the acquisition of further observations that could correct them.

We introduce the Move with Error paradigm and present ERA as its instantiation, coupling revisable occupancy (Move2Error) with exploration from reachable viewpoints (Error2Move), complemented by target verification for the final approach and stopping decision.

We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors on three benchmarks, and show that the two core mechanisms transfer to existing navigation systems and another depth predictor.

3. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors on three benchmarks, and show that the two core mechanisms transfer to existing navigation systems and another depth predictor.

title: Ego2Flow: Benchmarking the Traffic-System Impact of Autonomous Driving on Maps Distilled from Real-World Roads
authors: Yu Dong,Weiying Shen,Hangyu Li,Shu Han,Hong Li,Xiangbo Gao,Keshu Wu,Zhengzhong Tu,Soyoung Ahn,Zhiyuan Liu,Xiaopeng Li
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
End-to-end autonomous driving is predominantly evaluated through ego-vehicle safety and task completion.
Its deployment in urban traffic, however, creates sustained interactions among vehicles whose collective effects remain insufficiently evaluated.
We introduce Ego2Flow, a closed-loop benchmark for assessing the traffic-system impact of autonomous driving on maps distilled from real-world cities.
To construct realistic 3D urban environments for sustained closed-loop traffic simulation,
we develop an agent-guided map distillation framework that integrates real-world maps and observations with complementary geographic information.
Through an iterative feedback mechanism and a traffic information graph that jointly guide scene generation,
the framework preserves lane topology, critical road geometry and decision-relevant visual conditions while simplifying nonessential details and completing unobserved regions.
Using our proposed framework, we generate and publicly release six CARLA maps from the Argoverse 2 dataset,
covering the corresponding real-world regions and enabling paired comparisons of driving behavior under real and simulated observations.
On these maps, Ego2Flow evaluates how autonomous driving policies affect traffic efficiency, safety, stability and energy consumption across diverse road structures.
Compared with existing construction methods, our framework achieves the lowest average displacement error between planning outputs from paired real and simulated observations.
We further benchmark representative driving policies to characterize their system-level impact on urban traffic.
Project Page: https://github.com/Fisher-007/Ego2Flow.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving learns policies that translate sensor observations into driving decisions and has emerged as a prominent paradigm in autonomous driving research [26, 14, 23, 21].
Closed-loop simulation is central to evaluating these policies because it captures the feedback between their actions and subsequent observations, revealing driving behavior that open-loop prediction metrics may fail to reflect [7, 9].
Within this closed-loop setting, existing driving benchmarks primarily assess the ego vehicle’s ability to navigate safely and complete its assigned task [3, 17, 1].
However, urban deployment raises a further question about the traffic produced by those decisions.
A policy’s ability to complete an individual trip does not establish how its widespread deployment would affect urban traffic systems.

Vehicle interactions carry the effects of a vehicle’s driving decision beyond the controlled vehicle.
For example, a vehicle’s braking can induce speed disturbances that propagate through a platoon and delay following vehicles.
Figure  illustrates this distinction: the same pedestrian crossing can induce different patterns of speed loss and spacing along a platoon, even when the leading vehicle completes the maneuver safely.
Autonomous driving policies should therefore avoid amplifying such disturbances and exacerbating delays for following vehicles.
Yet evaluating ego-vehicle performance alone cannot fully capture these collective effects.

Transferring driving control to algorithms also creates an opportunity to improve traffic-system outcomes that individual human drivers do not typically optimize for.
Learning-based control has improved traffic flow in simulation [33], and field experiments have shown that controlling a single vehicle can suppress stop-and-go waves in predominantly human-driven traffic [29].
However, experiments with commercial adaptive cruise control have also observed disturbance amplification [12].
These contrasting findings motivate the central question of Ego2Flow: how does a driving policy affect the traffic it joins, and does its control improve collective outcomes?

Evaluating these effects for sensor-based driving policies requires environments that preserve decision-relevant road and visual conditions while supporting sustained interactions among vehicles.
We introduce Ego2Flow, a closed-loop benchmark for assessing the traffic-system impact of autonomous driving on maps distilled from real-world roads.
As summarized in Fig. , it provides six CARLA [10] maps covering the corresponding Argoverse 2 (AV2) regions [32].
Across these diverse urban road environments, Ego2Flow assesses end-to-end driving policies through their effects on traffic efficiency, safety, stability and estimated energy consumption.

To support this evaluation, we develop an agent-guided map-distillation framework for constructing 3D urban environments.
Distillation focuses on faithfully retaining the road structure and visual cues that shape driving decisions,
while simplifying less relevant geometry and appearance instead of reproducing every scene detail.
A traffic information graph connects these priorities to source evidence and dependencies among road elements,

title: EViDS: An Environment--Vehicle Dynamics Integrated Simulation Platform for Intelligent Chassis Development
authors: Lu Xiong,Yiming Zhou,Xuge Hu,Yi Zhang,Haoran Lv,Chen Tang
abstract: The development of intelligent chassis increasingly requires the integration of environmental and perception information with high-fidelity vehicle dynamics to support environment-aware intelligent chassis control. However, existing autonomous-driving simulators and professional vehicle-dynamics tools are generally developed for different purposes, making it difficult to integrate environmental information, vehicle dynamics, and chassis algorithms. This paper proposes EViDS, an Environment–Vehicle Dynamics Integrated Simulation Platform for Intelligent Chassis Development. EViDS integrates CARLA-based environment and sensor simulation with CarSim-based high-fidelity vehicle dynamics. Reference-pose-based state alignment and multi-rate interaction maintain spatial and temporal consistency, while ray-casting-based tire–road interaction transfers environmental information to the vehicle-dynamics model. Scenario configuration, synchronized data acquisition, and algorithm interfaces further support intelligent chassis development. The platform is evaluated through environment–dynamics interaction tests with vehicle-dynamics consistency comparisons, together with intelligent chassis applications. Results show that EViDS preserves vehicle-dynamics characteristics, reliably transfers environmental information, and supports online closed-loop intelligent chassis control, providing a unified simulation basis for environment-aware intelligent chassis development and validation.
introduction:

Meanwhile, the growing complexity of chassis architectures and multi-actuator coordination further strengthens the need for integrating environmental information with high-fidelity vehicle dynamics [2]. Therefore, intelligent chassis development requires simulation frameworks that combine realistic driving environments with high-fidelity vehicle dynamics.

However, existing simulation platforms still have limitations in supporting intelligent chassis development. Autonomous-driving-oriented platforms, such as CARLA and PreScan, mainly focus on environment and perception simulation, while their built-in vehicle models provide limited fidelity for detailed chassis dynamics analysis and control validation [3, 4]. Vehicle-dynamics-oriented platforms, such as CarSim and Adams/Car, provide high-fidelity vehicle and tire models but generally lack realistic and configurable driving environments and perception capabilities [5]. Existing integrated simulation approaches still face challenges in simultaneously providing realistic autonomous-driving environments and high-fidelity vehicle dynamics [6]. These limitations hinder the integrated development of environment-aware intelligent chassis algorithms.

Moreover, coupling heterogeneous simulators requires addressing differences in simulation interfaces, state representations, and time-management mechanisms to ensure consistent cross-platform interaction [7]. (1) An integrated environment–vehicle dynamics co-simulation architecture is proposed, enabling closed-loop interaction between autonomous-driving environments and high-fidelity vehicle dynamics for intelligent chassis development.

(2) Cross-domain interaction mechanisms are developed, including reference-pose-based state alignment, multi-rate interaction, and ray-casting-based tire–road interaction, to maintain spatial and temporal consistency and transfer environmental information to the vehicle dynamics domain.

title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
authors: Christopher Malili
abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot’s own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by α=V/(V+s2)\alpha=V/(V+s^{2}), where s2s^{2} is the reading noise and VV the anchor’s error variance. VV belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates α\alpha. Measured once, VV predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded α\alpha in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower α\alpha went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured α\alpha predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals ±0.08\pm 0.08), although training noise predicts it equally well. introduction:
A robot that learns by imitation usually gets object positions from perception, and those estimates are noisy. Training on noisy observations is a common remedy: the learner sees the noise during training and learns to discount the reading. How much it discounts the reading matters, because that sets how much perception error reaches the actions. Yet no quantitative account predicts this discount for modern policy classes before they are trained.

The obvious candidate is errors-in-variables (EIV) regression. A least-squares learner whose input is measured with noise attenuates its response to that input by the reliability ratio Λ=Σ​(Σ+s2​I)−1\Lambda=\Sigma(\Sigma+s^{2}I)^{-1}, where Σ\Sigma is the spread of the true input and s2s^{2} the noise variance (Fuller 1987; Carroll et al. 2006). On two toy tasks with scripted experts, where the learner’s only clean input was the task phase, this prediction held up: it matched the learned gain on a held-out task and, after one failed attempt, predicted success at new configurations (Appendix B). We then pre-registered it for diffusion policies (Chi et al. 2023) on the robomimic Square task (Mandlekar et al. 2021), with Σ\Sigma estimated from the demonstrations.

It failed. The predicted ranking of the noise conditions held, but at 12 mm of noise the policies kept 23% of their clean sensitivity on the informative axis, where EIV predicted 86%. Rather than stop there, we ran a sequence of diagnostic tests, each with its decision rule written before its data (Section 5.2). They ruled out a mis-estimated spread, local memorization, within-demonstration noise structure (tested on the MLP) and recall of training placements.

What remained is a proprioceptive anchor. Demonstrators steer toward the object, so the robot’s own state carries information about where the object is. A learner that combines this anchor with the reading, weighting each by its reliability, responds to the reading with α=V/(V+s2)\alpha=V/(V+s^{2}), where VV is the anchor's error variance. This is the EIV formula with the right conditioning set. The catch is that VV belongs to the learner: linear and nearest-neighbour estimators of the Square demonstrations put the anchor’s error at about 30 mm, where the diffusion policies act as if it were 6 to 7 mm. So we measure VV once, from one noise-trained policy, and predict every other noise level.

Deployment raises a different question, because in closed loop the robot’s state is produced by the policy itself. A persistent reading offset is then indistinguishable from a displaced object, and the anchor cannot protect against it. We find that the open-loop protection does not survive, and that policies with lower α\alpha succeed less often. Figure 1 summarizes the mechanism.

Contributions:

A predictive law for sensitivity to perception noise. With VV measured at one noise level, α=V/(V+s2)\alpha=V/(V+s^{2}) predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two tasks, two learner classes and four new noise levels. Its mean absolute error was 0.025, with all ten within their registered tolerances (0.10, and 0.05 for one secondary); classical EIV’s was 0.37, with none within tolerance (Section 5.1).

A predictive law for sensitivity to perception noise. With VV measured at one noise level, α=V/(V+s2)\alpha=V/(V+s^{2}) predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two tasks, two learner classes and four new noise levels. Its mean absolute error was 0.025, with all ten within their registered tolerances (0.10, and 0.05 for one secondary); classical EIV’s was 0.37, with none within tolerance (Section 5.1).

A test that rules out noise inflation. A learner that acts as if the noise were larger, with no anchor, has a bias at clean readings of −(1−α)-(1-\alpha). A learner whose anchor is the conditional mean of the object position given the robot state has a small one. Measured biases are small on both tasks and both learners, −0.003-0.003 to −0.052-0.052 against −0.37-0.37 to −0.75-0.75 for noise inflation. Their size agrees with the conditional-mean value on Can and, within a wide interval, for the MLP on Square; for diffusion on Square it is smaller (Section 5.3).

The closed-loop cost. Sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded α\alpha in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, so none kept its open-loop protection. The stricter registered prediction, that every policy follows the offset fully, held for 8 of them, so that verdict is mixed. For the MLP the offset response matched the response to a real displacement of the object (r = 0.94, post hoc). For diffusion policies on Can, a registered prospective test at two new noise levels confirmed that open-loop α\alpha predicts closed-loop success, within 0.03 (95% intervals ±0.08\pm 0.08), although a curve in training noise predicts it as well (Section 5.4).

A complete pre-registration record. Every test’s rule and predicted numbers were written before its data, and the later registrations also record the hashes of the code that ran them. The record includes the failed benchmark and the tests whose registered verdicts were mixed or negative (Appendix A).

Scope: the robot experiments are in simulation (robosuite), with synthetic Gaussian noise on the object position, low-dimensional observations, 200 human demonstrations per task and two seeds per configuration. Section 6 discusses what this does and does not license.
