title: On the Utility of Pre-Trained Visual Representations for Policy Learning of Contact-Rich Insertion Tasks
authors: Leon Kim,Dinesh Jayaraman,Michael Posa
abstract: Visuomotor imitation learning has become a predominant paradigm for real-world robotic manipulation, yet it remains data-inefficient and brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by distilling priors from internet-scale data, but the “right” representation for robotics remains unresolved: existing studies span broad but sparse task distributions and reach conclusions that vary and even conflict, pointing to strong task and setting dependence. We examine this question by bringing a magnifying glass to a common contact-rich manipulation task: insertion. We compare representations from widely used vision foundation models against an explicit contact-centric representation on two closely related insertion tasks, perturb each along controlled axes of occlusion and physical tolerance, and test whether conclusions transfer to the real world. Task dependence proves to be more subtle than previous, broadly scoped evaluations revealed: the best representation differs even between our near-identical tasks, and small changes shift trends in unpredictable ways. Despite this variability, results across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the distinct value of spatially-grounded, and in particular, contact-centric information for contact-rich policy learning, while underscoring how difficult it is to estimate such cues reliably under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise. We hope these findings motivate further study of representations in contact-rich manipulation, along with advances in contact perception and its integration into visuomotor policy learning.
introduction:
Imitation learning has emerged as a predominant paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling hobbyists and researchers alike to train visuomotor policies for diverse real-world tasks [1, 2, 3, 4]. Yet state-of-the-art imitation learning remains brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts unless supported by laborious amounts of demonstration data. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by leveraging priors distilled from internet-scale datasets [5, 6, 7]. However, which representation is “best” for robotics remains hotly debated: studies to date have evaluated broad but sparse task distributions and reached conclusions that vary and even contradict one another, with most suggesting the answer is highly task- and setting-dependent [8, 9, 10, 11]. Consistent with this, modern robotics foundation models (RFMs) have not converged on a single recipe, instead adopting disparate pre-trained vision encoders [12, 13, 14].

This uncertainty is especially salient in fine-grained, contact-rich manipulation. Despite large demonstration datasets and state-of-the-art visual representations, RFMs still struggle with contact-rich behaviors, with performance often lagging behind that on gross motor skills and soft-object manipulation. Perhaps because of this difficulty, fine-grained, contact-rich manipulation remains underrepresented in robot learning: datasets and benchmarks largely emphasize reaching, pick-and-place, or articulated object manipulation where successful behaviors demand neither millimeter-level precision in positioning nor frequent contact mode transitions across different surfaces [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. When contact-rich tasks do appear, they are often posed with generous tolerances that avoid tight-fit failure modes.

We argue this gap persists because contact-rich tasks both amplify common challenges and introduce unique ones. Rigid-body contact yields stiff, highly sensitive dynamics where small errors can cause discontinuous outcomes. Tight tolerances and friction induce hard-to-recover failures (e.g., jamming and wedging) that are pervasive in real assemblies [21, 22]. Finally, during close proximity and contact, task-relevant surfaces and their gaps are frequently occluded, limiting visual feedback precisely when and where it is most needed. These challenges have motivated efforts to incorporate spatially-dense contact and proximity information of critical object surfaces from tactile (and sometimes visual) sensors into visuomotor policy learning [23, 24, 25, 26, 27], but its value relative to standard visual priors remains unclear.

In this work, we restrict the question of the “right” visual representation to contact-rich manipulation, specifically insertion, and ask: (1) Do general-purpose vision foundation model (VFM) features (e.g., DINOv2 [5], SAM-2 [28], Theia [29]) improve policy performance over training from scratch? (2) Can explicit contact-centric information outperform VFMs, and under what conditions? Prior studies have pursued such questions over broad sets of disparate tasks, drawing preliminary conclusions that contact-rich tasks will benefit more from contact representations [23, 27].
These studies are beneficial for surveying the landscape of manipulation tasks, but we argue here that this breadth obscures the severity of the very task-dependence they report. Here, we specifically study a narrow domain, two similar insertion tasks, where previous studies would have reasonably indicated that contact features would bring value to both tasks. By evaluating policies in a narrow task domain, we are able to identify and highlight the surprising sensitivity in our findings to subtle changes in these tasks. To expose setting-dependent sensitivity, we perturb tasks along controlled axes: camera viewpoint shifts that modulate occlusion, and the tightness of physical tolerances. Finally, we extend our evaluation to the real world, where visual complexity and sensor noise provide further nuance to simulation results.

As this manuscript will detail, our results identify a surprising level of sensitivity, often defying traditional expectations. (1) In keeping with published results, we fully expected VFMs, particularly the robotics-tailored Theia, to substantially improve policy performance. However, while at least one VFM managed to provide substantial gains in most settings, the best-performing representation differed across tasks: Theia performed best in our real-world task but consistently matched baselines across simulated ones. Meanwhile, segmentation masks performed best in one simulated task but degraded once we introduced occlusions.
(2) Regarding contact-specific features, we hypothesized that explicit contact information would be more useful than common VFMs. Ground-truth (GT) contact information indeed consistently outperformed other representations across all settings, pointing to the critical importance of directly collocated tactile-like spatial features. However, when occlusions were minimal, segmentation masks performed just as well. Furthermore, estimated contact features struggled to match the performance of their ground-truth counterparts when faced with heavy occlusions or real-world sensor noise.

In sum, our contributions are as follows:

We take a hotly contested question in robot learning, restrict it to fine-grained, contact-rich insertion tasks, and demonstrate that the benefit of pre-trained visual representations is even less predictable than previously suggested.

Our results highlight not only that the best representation is highly task-dependent, but that seemingly small variations in a task can affect trends in unpredictable ways.

Despite this variability, our study provides evidence that contact information can offer distinct value, while also underscoring the practical challenge of inferring it reliably under occlusion and sensor noise.

title: TouchTwin: Scaling Human Touch Data via Real-to-Sim-to-Real
authors: Huiwen Han,Nuo Chen,Ziyao Zeng,Dayou Li,Hao Wang,Amir Hossein Rahmati,Xiaoning Qian,Bangya Liu,Zhiwen Fan
abstract: Human demonstrations are becoming the main source of data for dexterous manipulation, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines multiply each demonstration in simulation. These pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers how the hand moves. Which fingers touch, when, and how hard remain unobserved, because a hand pose shows where each finger stops on the surface rather than how far it is driven to close. This gap is a force gap: on held-out recordings, a hand policy that imitates the observed pose grips with 0.31×\times the recorded force, and a policy trained on physics replays of vision-tracked poses grips with 1.55×\times. TouchTwin closes the gap with measured human touch. Each selected TouchScale recording, captured with head and wrist RGB-D cameras and an 880-taxel glove, is rebuilt in MuJoCo. Coding agents write the objects as physics-tested programs, and a per-subject tactile hand replays the interaction with the recorded touch setting the contact and the closing force of each finger. In simulation, a policy trained on touch-grounded replays grips at 0.99×\times the recorded force and succeeds in 20/20 trials on held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations; a contact predictor trained on them misses 13% of real contact frames, against 32% for vision-based replays. Each replay also seeds perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered as realistic video in new views and scenes.
introduction:
Human demonstrations are the easiest dexterous manipulation data to collect at scale, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines rebuild them in simulation, where one recording seeds many (Wang et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2026; Dan et al., 2025; Allshire et al., 2025). However, these pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers only how the hand moves, how the object moves, or both. Contact force never enters the simulation, since video cannot observe it (Zhou et al., 2026b). A hand pose shows where each finger stops, not how far it closes, which sets grip force, and contacts are often hidden. Video thus misses which fingers touch, when, and how hard, and its two standard uses fail in opposite directions. In our experiments, pose imitation grips with 0.31×\times the recorded force, and replays built from vision with 1.55×\times. Physics alone does not recover the human grip either. In our touch-grounded replays of the mug pick-up task, the recorded grip is 1.6–3.7×\times the smallest force required to hold the mug. Touch measures this quantity (Sundaram et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2022; Song et al., 2025).

Gloves and other wearables have been used to model hand-object dynamics (Zhang et al., 2021), map touch to and from video (Zeng et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zeng et al., 2026b), supervise robot policies (Luo et al., 2026; Ni et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025) and identify object dynamics (Engelbracht et al., 2026), but none rebuilds the hand-object interaction as a physics simulation driven by measured touch, which lets one recording be replayed under new conditions. We build a data engine whose replays seed perturbed demonstrations and realistic video with contact and force labels, scaling scarce touch data without additional capture.

title: X-Nav Technical Report: Real-World Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor Navigation on a Humanoid Robot
authors: Jiaxin Huang,Chengxing Lin,Xiaoyu Luo,Sirui Chen,Jingyu Guo,Aolin Li,Kairui Chen,Rui Zhen,Cheng Wen,Kerui Gu,Shunyao Wang,Zhihui Peng,Shaoli Huang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
A humanoid robot that works in the real world must first reach its place of work.
Given one instruction, for example to go outside and buy a coffee at a store in a neighbouring building, it has to cross rooms, pass through doors, and walk along roads to its destination.
We refer to such a task as a mission.
AGIBOT measures productive robot work by Worken, the product of active robots, autonomous working hours, and output efficiency (AGIBOT, 2026), and each factor depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously.
This report studies missions in which a humanoid robot walks about a hundred metres from indoors to outdoors (Figure 1).
Vision-language navigation (VLN) formalises this task: an agent follows a language instruction using its visual observations (Anderson et al., 2018).
Progress on its benchmarks has been rapid.
Navigation models built on video-based vision–language models have raised the success rate on the continuous-environment benchmarks R2R-CE and RxR-CE year after year (Krantz et al., 2020; Ku et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026b; Zeng et al., 2026).
On R2R-CE it rose from 37% to above 70% within two years (Table 4), and on RxR-CE the best reported system now matches the success rate of human followers (Zhou et al., 2026a).
Over the same period, training sets grew to more than ten million samples (Zhang et al., 2026c; Zhou et al., 2026a), and real-robot deployments came to include quadrupeds and humanoids (Cheng et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026).

Has embodied navigation had its “GPT moment”?
On the benchmarks, it looks that way; on real robots, not yet.
Where a route length is reported, real-robot runs cover a few tens of metres (Zhang et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2026).
Reported trials on humanoids stay either indoors or outdoors (Cheng et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026), and systems that cover larger sites follow a route from map software or from a spatial memory built in advance (Tan et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026b).
To our knowledge, no reported system has taken a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed mission of about a hundred metres across the indoor–outdoor boundary.

Why do high scores in simulation fail to carry over to real robots?
We trace the gap to three places: the problem that a benchmark poses, the data that models learn from, and the step from a trained model to a walking robot.
We start with the problem: a benchmark episode is a narrower task than a mission.
An episode covers ten to fifteen metres inside a single building.
The scene is a scan, the camera is simulated and stays at a fixed height, every step is executed exactly as commanded, nothing else in the scene moves, and stopping anywhere within three metres of the goal counts as success.
A mission on a humanoid breaks each of these assumptions.
The route is several times as long and leaves the building, where walls a few metres away give way to open ground and buildings tens of metres away.
The camera moves with the gait, and the step that the robot takes can differ from the one commanded.
People, carts, and cars cross its path.
Nor is stopping within three metres good enough: a robot sent to a store has to arrive at its entrance.
A high score therefore shows that a model follows instructions under benchmark conditions; it says little about the conditions that the benchmark leaves out.
We therefore take the mission itself as the problem, and define it as follows.
A bipedal humanoid receives an instruction in natural language, and the instruction may change during the mission.
Its navigation model sees only RGB images from the robot’s built-in camera, and the robot has neither a map of the site nor a reference route.
The route is about a hundred metres long, starts indoors, and ends outdoors, with static and dynamic obstacles along the way.
The mission is complete when the robot stops at the destination named in the instruction.

Will more data close the gap?
Scaling up the training set has been the usual response (Zhang et al., 2026c; Zhou et al., 2026a), and it does push benchmark scores up.
But the data are the second place where the gap opens, because a sample can teach only what it contains.
Standard VLN data are collected in scanned indoor scenes with a simulated camera (Chang et al., 2017), the same kind of setting that the benchmarks use.
Such samples contain neither the site where the robot will work nor the robot’s own camera, gait, and stopping behaviour, and adding more of them cannot supply what is missing.
Reference routes also show only correct behaviour, whereas a model on a long route has to recover from its own mistakes.
More is better only when it adds what is missing: the first question is what kind of data, not how much.

What kind of data does a humanoid need, and where should it come from?
Working back from what the model has to learn, we find three needs, each met by a different source.
First, the model has to follow instructions across many kinds of scenes and routes.
This calls for scale and diversity, and open-source scenes in simulation supply both.
Second, the model has to work at the site where the robot is deployed.
This calls for the layout and appearance of that site: a scan turns the site into a digital twin, in which routes are collected and the model is run so that its mistakes can be corrected (Ross et al., 2011) before the robot sets foot there.
Third, the model has to work on this particular robot.
This calls for the robot’s own camera views and motion, which recordings on the real robot capture directly.

In simulation and in the twin, each sample pairs the camera view with an instruction and with supervision that matches both: the next actions or a navigation goal.
The three sources differ in size by orders of magnitude, from 6.3M samples in open-source scenes to a few hundred routes at a single site, and each supplies what the others lack.
As for how much is enough, we judge it where the robot works, in closed loop in the twin and on the robot, rather than on the benchmark alone.
In the twin of an office lobby, a few hundred routes adapt the model to the site, and adding correction data raises its closed-loop success rate from 40% to 80% (Section 7.2).

What does it take to put the model on a real robot?
Deployment is the third place where the gap opens: a trained model is not yet a robot that walks.
The first decision is the camera.
Real-robot deployments commonly mount an additional camera on the robot, such as an Intel RealSense D455 (Zhang et al., 2025a; Wei et al., 2026b; Wei et al., 2026a); a model that uses the robot’s built-in camera leaves the hardware untouched.
The rest is what a mission asks for beyond the output of a model: a brief instruction has to be divided into sub-tasks, each stop has to be checked, a predicted goal has to stay valid while the robot keeps walking, static and dynamic obstacles have to be avoided, and the last few metres to a named target have to be covered.

What, in the end, should a framework for real-world humanoid navigation look like?
It has to close the gap in all three places: to take the mission, rather than the benchmark episode, as its problem; to collect data that contain the site and the robot; and to carry the model all the way onto the robot.
Such a framework is more than a model: it covers the full pipeline from data to deployment, and it is tested on the robot itself.

This report presents X-Nav, a navigation system built along these lines (Figure 1).
The data engine collects navigation data from the three sources: open-source scene collection at scale, digital-twin collection at the deployment site, and real-robot collection on the Lingxi X2 humanoid.
MELIOR , the navigation model, takes only RGB images from the built-in camera of the Lingxi X2 and requires no additional camera.
It comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal.
X-Navarch , the agentic workflow, deploys MELIOR on the robot: a planner divides a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and reviews each stop, MELIOR follows each route, the explicit navigation skill MELIOR-X approaches a named target over the last metres, and an obstacle-avoidance layer operates between the navigation goal and the locomotion controller.
X-Navarch uses no map of the site; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control.
On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building with both versions of MELIOR: a run of 96.6 m with MELIOR-A, and a run with X-Navarch and MELIOR-N that encounters static and dynamic obstacles (Section 7.1).
In an office lobby, the data engine and MELIOR-A close the loop from a scan to the robot: the model is adapted with data collected in the digital twin of the lobby, and the adapted model drives the Lingxi X2 in the real lobby (Section 7.2).
On R2R-CE and RxR-CE, MELIOR is competitive with recent models that use one forward camera (Section 7.3).
Our contributions are as follows.

We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first navigation system that takes a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors.

title: Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
authors: Arne Sachtler,Manuel Keppler,Florian Loeffl,Alin Albu-Schäffer
abstract: Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them. We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6 % of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint. The constraint uses the model-based rate of the error, so no stabilizing feedback gain is needed. Experiments in hardware show swing-ups along both modes and compare the allocation with summing-and-clipping and with prioritized stabilization.
introduction:
We want robots whose wanted motions are natural motions of their dynamics, and nonlinear normal modes (NNMs) are one way to embed them: control uses what is already there instead of forcing new dynamics onto the system. Our control approach holds for nn joints and their nn modes; we show it on two, whose modes are easy to understand and to visualize.

Swinging up a robot whose motors cannot even hold its arm horizontal is a matter of timing, not of force. The direct-drive motors of the planar two-link robot of Fig. 1 deliver only 1.11.1 Nm, about 6 % of the gravity torque in the first joint with the arm held horizontally. With full torque in both joints, link 2 tilts by 16.3∘16.3^{\circ} and link 1 stays hanging, because the reaction of the elbow torque cancels the shoulder torque (Fig. 1b). Neither a joint PD controller nor a controller that tracks a direct path to the upright pose (Fig. 5a) can get there; the robot has to collect the energy over many swings. A single pendulum is swung up by energy control, which puts it on the homoclinic orbit that ends upright [1]. The double pendulum is chaotic [2], so energy control alone most likely ends in chaotic motion, and energy-based swing-ups of double pendulums pass through intermediate equilibria [3, 4]. We instead guide the swing-up along the NNMs of the robot [5, 6, 7], families of periodic orbits of the free dynamics, one per energy. On one mode the robot behaves much like a single pendulum: there is no chaos, and the modes connect the hanging equilibrium to a homoclinic orbit at the upright one [8]. Pumping energy along a mode thus carries the robot from rest to almost upright, where a short precomputed trajectory catches it in a handstand.

Like earlier work, we ride a mode with two control loops, one that keeps the state on the mode and one that changes the energy. Both share the same limited motor torques, a box of admissible torques with one bound per joint, which we call the box constraint. Prior work sums the two loops [9, 10], gives priority to stabilization [8], or solves a nonlinear MPC in simulation [11]. The loops interfere: a torque that corrects the error with respect to the mode generally does work and changes the energy. On a non-strict mode, one whose orbits do not all run along the same path in configuration space, no bounded torque can change the energy while keeping the state on the mode [12, Thm. 1], and the modes of our robot are non-strict (Sec. II-D). Power-neutral steering is known from gyroscopic forces [13], power-continuous curve tracking [14] and geometric fabrics [15], and pumping along the momentum stays on a strict mode [16]. What is not known is how to allocate the two under a box constraint on a non-strict mode, where pumping leaves the mode and steering must undo it.

We split the input torque by its power into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: pump as hard as the box allows, subject to one control-Lyapunov function (CLF) constraint [17] that makes a transverse error measure decay. Unlike classical control allocation [18], there is no actuator redundancy; we allocate the torque box between two tasks. No feedback gains are designed; the transverse instability of the orbits sets the decay rate. The PD stabilizers of earlier mode-based swing-ups [9, 10, 8] and transverse feedback linearization of orbits [19, 20] need gains tuned against the pumping, and optimal orbit stabilization [21] handles a single orbit with unbounded inputs, not a family under a tight box constraint.

A gain-free controller that excites and stabilizes a mode with limited torque: one linear program allocates pumping and power-neutral steering under the box constraint.

title: Grounding Object-to-Object Hazard Reasoning into 3D Risk Fields for Task-Conditioned Safety
authors: Mariana Sosa Guzmán,Yide Song,Amin Abyaneh,Gregory Dudek,Hsiu-Chin Lin
abstract: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io
introduction:
Robots that manipulate everyday objects must anticipate if and how their actions can cause harm. Doing so requires connecting what they see with what they are asked to do: an object’s properties, its surroundings, and its intended use together determine which interactions are hazardous. Collision avoidance provides an essential foundation [1, 2, 3, 4], but geometry alone is far from sufficient for identifying safety constraints. We study the broader challenge of contextual safety [5, 6, 7] in robotic manipulation, with the aim of enabling robots to derive safety constraints from the task and scene and utilize visual context and structured reasoning to guide task rejection and motion correction.

These ideas have been explored both in manipulation [5] and in navigation [6, 8, 7]. In navigation, constraints are defined over the regions the robot itself may occupy. In manipulation, the robot additionally acts on the environment through the object it holds, so safety depends on the relationship between that object and the remaining objects of the scene. For example, placing a metal cup in a microwave for heating can create a hazard regardless of the transport path, whereas carrying coffee over a laptop creates a hazard that can be avoided by routing the cup around it (Figure. 1). Hazard reasoning must therefore decide whether a task should be performed at all and, if so, which regions become hazardous for the manipulated object due to the task.

In prior work, this knowledge typically comes from a human who specifies the constraints [6, 8, 9, 10]
or from Hamilton-Jacobi reachability [11]. However, a predefined hazard set could not cover all possible hazards that arise in an open-world environment. There is increasing interest in extracting this contextual knowledge directly from large language models (LLMs). Existing work in manipulation segments visual input into a semantic map, uses a pretrained model to reason about safe and unsafe behavior, and enforces the resulting constraints through control barrier functions (CBFs) [5]; however, reducing the scene to a language representation limits the context available for reasoning. Vision-language models (VLMs) jointly process semantic and visual information, allowing reasoning over objects, attributes, and relationships within a scene. This direction has been explored for navigation [7], but its application to hazards induced by object interactions in manipulation remains underexplored.

Knowing what is unsafe, however, does not by directly prevent it. Safety filters such as CBFs [12, 13] provide formal guarantees that corrected nominal trajectories to keep the robot safe with respect to spatially unsafe sets, under their respective modeling and control assumptions. These sets and rules must be specified in advance. Foundation models inherit a high-level semantic understanding to reason about potential hazard interactions, but their predictions need grounding to be applied.
A hazard detection pipeline must therefore bridge these two ideas: it must reason about safety based on the environment and task, and ground the predicted hazards in a representation that a classical filter can act on continuously.

In this work, we propose a framework centered around a VLM with visual context and a text description of the task to detect hazards arising from interactions between objects and induced by the robot’s actions. A structured schema-based toolset first determines whether the task should be rejected and, otherwise, outputs object-pair hazards with geometric restrictions. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth ground these restrictions in an automatically generated 3D risk field, which an obstacle modulation filter uses to correct the manipulated object’s motion. In parallel, we present a systematic study of how context representation and structured reasoning affect pretrained models for object-to-object hazard detection.
Our contributions are:

A structured VLM safety toolset that separates task rejection from identifying preventable object-pair hazards, and outputs geometric restrictions that can be grounded in the scene.

An automatically generated 3D risk field, built from open-vocabulary segmentation and depth, that represents non-convex hazard geometry without fitting shape primitives, and connects VLM hazard reasoning to obstacle modulation.

A study of context representation and structured hazard reasoning, identifying false-rejection failures and evaluating downstream safe execution in simulation and real-world manipulation.

We evaluate our methodology in simulation and real-world experiments, comparing it against task-only reasoning, reasoning over scene descriptions, and geometric obstacle modulation. The evaluation covers tasks requiring rejection, preventable hazards, and safe variants, assessing both hazard avoidance and task completion.

1. A structured VLM safety toolset that separates task rejection from identifying preventable object-pair hazards, and outputs geometric restrictions that can be grounded in the scene.

2. An automatically generated 3D risk field, built from open-vocabulary segmentation and depth, that represents non-convex hazard geometry without fitting shape primitives, and connects VLM hazard reasoning to obstacle modulation.

3. A study of context representation and structured hazard reasoning, identifying false-rejection failures and evaluating downstream safe execution in simulation and real-world manipulation.

title: Talk to Act: A Synthetic Multi-Turn Dialogue Benchmark for Human Intent Extraction and Action Planning in Robotics
authors: Deepu Krishnareddy,Mohammad Haziq Khan,Michael Danner,Matthias Rätsch

abstract: Multi-turn conversational human–robot interaction (HRI) continues to be a challenging problem in robotics, as many existing systems rely on rigid, command-driven interfaces that can be unintuitive for users. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a promising direction, given their ability to process natural language, generate structured outputs, and support tool-based reasoning, all of which are relevant for interpreting user intent in robotic settings. However, progress in this area is constrained by the limited availability of datasets and benchmarks that capture the nuances of real-world human communication, such as multi-turn dialogue, ambiguity, and context-dependent requests.
introduction:
Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) has emerged as a critical frontier in robotics, enabling robots to operate alongside humans in shared environments such as assisted living facilities, warehouses, and domestic settings. As robots move from controlled industrial cells into homes, care environments, and shared workspaces, communication becomes a core capability rather than a peripheral interface.

In recent years, substantial progress has been made in robotics, particularly in perception and control. Large embodied datasets and generalist robot policies have advanced robotic performance. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have demonstrated the effectiveness of web-scale pretraining in enhancing semantic generalization in robotic control. However, interaction between humans and robots is still unnatural. A robot that is capable of perceiving objects and executing movements with precision may still struggle when a user makes an underspecified, multistep, or revised request in everyday language.

Nevertheless, natural language is the most intuitive communication medium for people. Previous studies have contrasted natural language with complex graphical interfaces, structured command languages, and formal abstractions, which require training before a user can effectively control a robot. For robots in homes, assistive scenarios, or shared human environments, it is often unrealistic to expect the human to learn a rigid interaction protocol. A more realistic objective is for robots to be able to interpret natural, unconstrained, and potentially messy human language as it is actually spoken. However, unrestricted language is challenging because human requests are often context-dependent, incomplete, and ambiguous.

Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have introduced new opportunities for integrating natural language into robotic tasks. Models such as GPT-5, Claude and Gemini demonstrate strong capabilities in common sense reasoning, following instructions, and tool calling — properties that are directly relevant to interpreting user intent and translating it into structured robot actions. LLMs ability to handle compositional instructions and generate structured outputs makes LLMs a promising foundation for the interaction layer. Furthermore, LLMs offer a promising approach to generating synthetic data, enabling the creation of extensive and diverse dialogue corpora that would otherwise be too costly to collect through human annotation.

Although LLMs have great potential in HRI, existing approaches tend to reduce interaction to single-turn intent extraction within narrowly defined task domains [1]. However, real human communication is multi-turn, context-dependent, and often under-specified. Users revise goals, refer to objects implicitly, and issue instructions that are only interpretable when considering the prior conversational context.

While large frontier models may be attractive for intent understanding due to their strong reasoning capabilities, their deployment in robotic systems is constrained by latency, connectivity requirements, cost, and privacy considerations. In contrast, recent compact open-weight models such as Phi-4, Gemma series, and Qwen series demonstrate that smaller models are becoming increasingly capable at instruction following and structured output generation, making them compelling candidates for on-device or edge-assisted HRI pipelines. Whether such models can reliably handle the full complexity of natural, multi-turn human dialogue in HRI contexts, however, remains an open question.

Alongside language, perception capabilities have also advanced significantly. Modern models such as SAM 3 [2] and Grounded DINO [3] now support open-vocabulary segmentation and detection driven by natural language queries. Yet current HRI systems rarely leverage these capabilities, leaving a gap between what perception models can accept and what interaction pipelines actually provide. A well-designed dialogue system that extracts structured referential expressions from human conversation could directly bridge this gap, feeding natural language grounded outputs into modern perception models.

A key bottleneck in advancing natural language-based HRI is the lack of datasets that reflect the complexity of real human communication. Existing benchmarks are limited in scale, domain diversity, and conversational depth. To address this, we introduce a synthetically generated multi-turn dialogue dataset for HRI, designed to capture natural, ambiguous, and context-dependent human instructions annotated with action intent, action plans, and object intent. The dataset spans a variety of real-world scenarios and user personas, reflecting the diversity of people and contexts a robot may encounter in practice. We further present an initial benchmark of small open-weight language models on this dataset, exploring their ability to extract user intent and task plans from unconstrained human dialogue in HRI settings.

title: Learning Latent Goal Costs for Visual World-Model Planning with an Expanding Curriculum
authors: Konstantinos Mylonas,Thrasyvoulos Spyropoulos
abstract: Image-goal planning with a frozen visual world model depends on how predicted observations are scored against the goal. Mean-squared error (MSE) between embeddings from a pretrained visual encoder can provide a useful signal near a goal, yet favor states across an obstacle that are visually similar to the goal and difficult to reach. We fit a small residual adapter on top of frozen I-JEPA embeddings to improve this latent goal cost. Starting near each goal, a planner collects trajectories from progressively wider regions of initial states. The adapter learns from the order of observations along successful trajectories, with additional comparisons inferred from failed rollouts. No task-specific progress labels are used for fitting, so the procedure can be applied to other goal-reaching tasks. the DotWall and PointMaze used in this work. In paired 50-case evaluations with identical starts, goals, world models, and planner settings, success increases from 54% to 98% in DotWall and from 82% to 96% in PointMaze. On 16 unseen DotWall layout–goal cases, the adapter fitted on one fixed layout improves agreement between latent-cost ordering and shortest legal-path ordering from 71.9% to 85.8%. The results indicate that planning experience can improve a frozen visual representation’s goal cost without retraining the encoder or the world model.
introduction:
World models have long been useful for decision making and control because they let an agent predict the consequences of its actions before acting [1, 2]. Visual latent world models make these predictions in a learned latent space: they predict the next latent state from previous latent states and actions. Once the model has learned the environment’s dynamics, a planner can roll out candidate action sequences and score their predicted outcomes against a goal. In closed-loop model predictive control, the agent executes the first action of the selected plan, receives a new observation, and replans. Predicting in latent space avoids expensive pixel reconstructions and allows many action sequences to be evaluated efficiently.

Planning this way still presents two challenges. Errors accumulate when a world model is rolled out for many steps, limiting how far ahead it can predict reliably. Separately, the latent cost between a predicted state and the goal need not reflect how difficult it is to reach the goal from that state. This is particularly relevant when a world model uses a pretrained, task-agnostic visual encoder, as in DINO-WM, which uses DINOv2 to encode image frames [3, 4]. The resulting embeddings can capture visual similarity without encoding the travel required by a particular task. Consider DotWall in Fig. 1. The ball can appear close to the goal across the wall, even though it has to travel through the doorway to reach the other room. A planner using raw latent cost may therefore favor a state that looks promising, although in reality it is difficult to reach the goal from it [5].

We study this problem with a world model built on a pretrained I-JEPA encoder [6]. Pretrained visual encoders have useful spatial and geometric features that extend beyond one navigation task [6, 4]. We keep the I-JEPA encoder and world model fixed, and fit a small adapter to the encoder’s latent representations so that their distance to the goal guides planning better than the raw latent cost. In DotWall and PointMaze, we know what an ideal measure of progress looks like: geodesic distance decreases along a shortest legal route to the goal. We could supervise the adapter with that distance, but doing so would build our knowledge of these particular environments into the method. For other tasks, the right measure of progress may be difficult to define—for example, when a robot must arrange scattered blocks into a target shape. We therefore propose a task-agnostic training procedure that aims to discover a useful measure of progress from experience, rather than fitting an adapter to targets specified using our expert knowledge of each task.

Our approach builds on an observation: close to the goal, the raw latent cost often has enough structure to guide the planner successfully. We first collect trajectories from starting positions near the goal. A successful trajectory eventually reaches the goal, so the order of its observations provides a weak signal of progress: observations visited later tend to be closer to completing the task than those visited earlier. We fit the adapter so that later observations have lower adapted latent cost to the goal, while recognizing that this ordering need not hold at every step. We then collect trajectories from progressively farther starting positions and repeat, using each updated adapter to guide the next stage.

In matched 50-case planning evaluations, the adapted latent cost increases success from 54% to 98% in DotWall and from 82% to 96% in PointMaze. We also evaluate the DotWall adapter on 16 cases from unseen environment layouts, where the wall and doorway have moved from their positions during training. Its latent cost agrees more closely with geodesic distance on these layouts, improving legal-path pair ordering from 71.9% to 85.8%.

Our contributions are:

We show how raw I-JEPA latent cost can misguide a CEM-based planner and measure the resulting planning failures.

We propose a task-agnostic curriculum for fitting a small, task-specific latent adapter from collected trajectories, without supervision on expert targets.

We show that the adapter improves planning in two environments. Moreover, the adapted latent cost in DotWall generalizes to unseen environment layouts: it agrees closely with the geodesic distance that describes progress in this task, even when the wall and doorway change position.

title: Racing the Clock: Teaching VLNs Budget-Conditioned Object Search
authors: Maitree Meher,Siming He,S. Shankar Sastry,Jitendra Malik,Claire Tomlin,Jonas Frey
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: How do action budgets shape vision-language navigation (VLN) exploration, and what expert supervision best teaches budget-aware search? We study budget-conditioned object search: finding as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within a budget, with discovery defined geometrically by camera field of view and proximity. Distinct discoveries provide a denser evaluation signal than single-target success. We cast expert design as a choice of scene abstraction: a single budget-indexed Bellman recursion, applied to different abstractions of the full environment, yields experts that differ in what they know. An object-level Bellman expert is given every target location and reduces search to budgeted routing. A room-level Bellman expert retains observed room connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene semantic priors but withholds the contents of unexplored rooms, so it must search for targets that its student also cannot see. We distill both experts into Uni-NaVid under matched training conditions and also evaluate greedy-frontier supervision on held-out HM3D scenes. Changing only the stated budget changes learned trajectories. Despite higher object-level expert return, room-level supervision achieves the highest mean collection among evaluated VLNs at every tested budget. At 2000 steps, it finds 72.7% of reachable targets, versus 68.5% under greedy-frontier supervision, 65.5% under object-level supervision, and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results show that expert-return rankings need not predict supervision quality for VLN exploration, and motivate choosing an expert’s abstraction with the student’s information in mind rather than by expert return alone.
introduction:
An indoor search robot must allocate its budget between nearby targets and distant regions: a short budget may favor immediate collection, while a longer one may justify travel to a promising room. To assess both effective budget use and its influence on decisions, we first ask: how does the available budget change where and how a vision-language navigation (VLN) policy searches?

This motivates budget-conditioned object search: finding as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within an action budget. The agent receives RGB history, a target instruction, and a remaining-budget countdown, but no complete map or unseen target locations. Travel, scanning, and target approach consume budget. We count an instance as collected when it meets geometric proximity and camera-field-of-view criteria, without physical pickup. Distinct discoveries provide a denser signal than binary success and preserve repeated choices between visible targets and further exploration. Collection across budgets measures search performance; controlled countdown interventions test behavioral sensitivity (Fig. 1).

The remaining horizon can change the optimal action despite identical observation histories [1]; omitting it creates state aliasing between short-horizon collection and longer-horizon exploration. Although finite-resource planning is well studied, pretrained VLNs such as Uni-NaVid [2] lack an explicit remaining-budget countdown. In a NaVILA [3] pilot, a shorter stated limit sometimes produced more actions than a longer one, motivating budget-aware demonstrations beyond merely adding a prompt limit.

To assess what supervision best transfers to a partially observed student, we next ask:
what kind of expert demonstrations effectively teach budget-conditioned search? A full-map expert can route efficiently yet prescribe different actions in environments indistinguishable to the student, an information mismatch that can hinder asymmetric imitation [4, 5, 6, 7].
Prior work addresses this mismatch by modifying the imitation objective or by adapting the expert to the student. We ask a complementary question: what environmental information should the planning expert itself retain when generating exploration supervision?

Existing exploration methods span different information regimes. Experts with full map and target-location access [8, 9] reduce search to routing among known goals, while receding-horizon planners [10, 11, 12, 13] act from currently available information but may provide weak long-horizon guidance. Scene-prediction methods inject priors about unseen regions [14, 15], but predicting detailed unseen geometry and semantics is itself challenging.

We make this information choice explicit. An expert plans over an abstraction z=φ⁡(ℳ)z=\varphi(\mathcal{M}) of the full environment ℳ\mathcal{M} and knows only the part of zz revealed to it so far; one budget-indexed Bellman recursion over this information state then defines the expert. Varying φ\varphi spans a spectrum of information access. Revealing every target location yields an object-level Bellman expert that routes among known targets: nothing is left to search for. Retaining observed room connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene semantic priors while withholding the contents of unexplored rooms yields a room-level Bellman expert, for which each unentered room is a search opportunity with uncertain yield and delayed reward. Withholding unseen contents, not the room granularity itself, is what turns room selection into search. It also determines what the student is asked to imitate: object-level actions can depend on targets the student has not seen, whereas room-level actions depend only on information the student could acquire by exploring. Multi-room search preserves the key choice between a visible target and a room with uncertain, delayed reward.

Equal target values and unit primitive-action costs isolate these questions from target priorities and cost weights, while collection and uncertain exploration still compete for finite budget. Our focus is supervision and budget use within a fixed video VLN architecture: both Bellman experts supervise Uni-NaVid students that predict primitive actions from RGB history and language, and a greedy frontier expert and its supervised VLN provide coverage-oriented comparisons. Our goal is not to replace explicit-map exploration methods such as frontier planning; we use them as references for what explicit spatial memory achieves.

All three expert-supervised VLNs use matched scenes, budgets, and record counts; the two Bellman students also use identical optimization. Room-level supervision achieves the highest mean collection at every budget in ten held-out HM3D scenes despite lower expert return. Budget-blind controls distinguish countdown gains from supervision-source differences; countdown interventions test behavioral sensitivity. These findings motivate recording demonstration budgets and considering expert search behavior when choosing supervision.

Our contributions are:

We formulate budget-conditioned object search, using distinct target collection to measure effective budget use and controlled countdown interventions to assess behavioral sensitivity to the budget.

We formalize expert design as a choice of abstraction φ\varphi of the full environment. One budget-indexed Bellman recursion then spans fully informed routing and search under uncertainty, and the abstraction makes explicit which information enters the expert’s actions and must be imitated by a partially observed student.

We instantiate a room-level Bellman expert that withholds the contents of unexplored rooms and estimates this recursion from strictly cross-scene transitions, providing budget-conditioned search demonstrations for a VLN.

We compare room-level, fully informed object-level, and greedy-frontier supervision for Uni-NaVid on matched scenes, budgets, and record counts. Room-level supervision yields the highest mean collection, while higher expert return need not yield a stronger student.

title: Agentic-Teacher: An Agentic Data Engine for Failure-Driven VLA Post-Training
authors: Gongyue Teng,Yuqing Xie,Yixian Zhang,Feng Gao,Shu'ang Yu,Jiaji Rao,Sukai Wang,Guanghui Ren,Ya Zhang,Maoqing Yao,Yu Wang,Chao Yu,Xinlei Chen
abstract: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model’s flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves π0\pi_{0} success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.
introduction:
During deployment, vision-language-action (VLA) policies may encounter states outside their training distribution due to environmental noise or accumulated control errors, potentially leading to task failure. DAgger addresses this distribution shift by collecting expert actions at states visited by the learned policy and aggregating them for further training (Ross et al., 2011). Obtaining this supervision from human experts requires repeated monitoring and intervention. Although HG-DAgger and ThriftyDAgger improve takeover mechanisms and intervention allocation, they still depend on human corrections (Kelly et al., 2019; Hoque et al., 2022), making corrective learning costly to scale across tasks and environments.

Advances in multimodal understanding, code generation, and tool use have enabled coding agents to construct and refine robot behaviors through environment interaction. Code as Policies connects language-model-generated programs to perception and control interfaces (Liang et al., 2022). Within this tool-based execution paradigm, Harness VLA exposes a frozen VLA as a callable manipulation primitive alongside analytic controllers, enabling agents to coordinate learned and programmed behaviors without policy fine-tuning (Zhang et al., 2026). To refine behaviors through environmental feedback, CaP-X, Act-Observe-Rewrite, and Agent as Policy incorporate observation, execution, and program revision into iterative feedback loops (Fu et al., 2026; Kumar, 2026; Jia et al., 2026). ASPIRE and Uni-Skill further support skill construction and reuse, enabling subsequent exploration to build on accumulated experience (Lu et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026).

A complementary line of work uses agents to support robot policy learning. RoboClaw coordinates self-resetting rollouts to collect training data and iteratively improve VLA skill policies (Li et al., 2026), while ENPIRE enables coding agents to manage real-world policy evaluation and refine training algorithms (Xiao et al., 2026). InSight acquires missing action primitives through guided interaction and incorporates successful demonstrations into VLA training (Wang et al., 2026). Recova develops task and recovery behaviors in digital twins and refines separate policies through real-world DAgger. This motivates using coding agents to autonomously construct corrective experts for a target VLA’s observed failures, reducing reliance on human-provided corrections. Our focus is on both generating successful corrective demonstrations and adapting them into effective supervision for VLA post-training.

This leads to our central question: Can coding agents autonomously identify the causal frame and reason from failure trajectories, generate successful repair demonstrations, and distill the resulting corrective behaviors back into the model? To answer this question, we introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine that acts as a teacher for failure-driven VLA post-training (Fig. 1). Rather than assuming access to a predefined expert capable of correcting every failure, Agentic-Teacher constructs localized code-policy experts on demand, targeting the specific weaknesses revealed by the VLA’s own execution.

title: CS-MPC: Contraction-Certified Sampling-Based MPC for Nonlinear Systems Under Uncertainty
authors: Yashwanth Kumar Nakka
abstract: We present contraction-certified sampling-based model predictive control (CS-MPC) for tracking and safety of nonlinear robotic systems under parametric uncertainty, disturbances, and safety constraints that are revealed online. CS-MPC uses a contraction-certified tracking feedback inside every sampled rollout, which concentrates the rollouts around the reference, and an execution layer that verifies the applied input using a quantile-tightened discrete-time control barrier function condition. We derive a verification procedure for nonlinear contraction of the feedback-closed dynamics, and we prove a finite-sample stochastic stability bound and a mission-level probabilistic safety guarantee. We validate CS-MPC in simulation on a rover, a quadrotor, and an asteroid landing. When compared with standard model predictive path integral (MPPI) control, CS-MPC attains the same tracking error with 7 to 20 times fewer rollouts for the rover, and a 2 to 4 times lower tracking error for the quadrotor, with no safety violations in 200 Monte Carlo missions.
introduction:
Planetary rovers [1, 2], spacecraft operating near small bodies [3], and agile aerial robots [4] must track a planned trajectory in environments that are only partially known before the mission. A rover follows a path over terrain with uncertain slip. A spacecraft descends toward a small body with uncertain gravity and spin. An aerial robot flies among moving obstacles that are detected only during flight. In each case, the dynamics are nonlinear, some model parameters are uncertain for the whole mission, the actuators have deadband or quantization, and some safety constraints are revealed only online. Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) [5, 6, 7] computes the control input from Monte Carlo rollouts of the dynamics, which allows nonsmooth and nonconvex mission costs to be optimized without gradients. However, standard model predictive path integral (MPPI) control [8] has three limitations for these problems. First, the rollouts are propagated in open loop, so they spread quickly when the dynamics are unstable, and many samples are needed for a useful control update. Second, the safety constraints enter as rollout penalties, which shape the sampling distribution but do not certify the input that is applied to the system. Third, the effect of a finite number of samples on the closed-loop tracking error is usually evaluated only in simulation.

In this work, we present contraction-certified sampling-based MPC (CS-MPC), which addresses these three limitations using two layers, as shown in Fig. 1. The stability and performance layer computes a tracking feedback gain and a contraction metric offline along the reference trajectory using a backward Riccati recursion [9, 10, 11], and verifies that the nonlinear closed-loop dynamics are contracting on a specified domain. CS-MPC uses this feedback inside every sampled rollout, which keeps the rollouts close to the reference, while the MPPI weights optimize the sampled feedforward input for nonsmooth mission costs. The execution layer verifies the weighted input before it is applied, using a discrete-time control barrier function (DCBF) condition [12, 13] that is tightened by a conditional quantile region for the one-step prediction error. If the weighted input does not satisfy this condition, then the execution layer applies a feasible sampled input or a backup policy. The analysis accounts for the persistent parameter uncertainty, the process noise, the actuator error, and the finite number of samples.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We derive an offline procedure that synthesizes the tracking feedback and verifies nonlinear contraction of the closed-loop dynamics over a specified domain, which gives nominal and stochastic tracking bounds. We prove that the spread of the feedback-closed rollouts is bounded uniformly in the horizon, which is the mechanism behind the sample efficiency observed in simulation.

We present an execution layer that verifies the applied input using a quantile-tightened DCBF condition, which handles nonconvex, nonsmooth, and time-varying safe sets. We prove a mission-level probabilistic safety guarantee when the prediction-error region is conditionally valid and a feasible backup policy is available.

We derive a concentration bound for the weighted control input and use it to prove a finite-sample stochastic stability bound for the closed-loop system, which separates the effects of the sample budget, the disturbances, and the avoidance maneuvers.

We validate CS-MPC in simulation on a rover under terrain-slip uncertainty, a quadrotor flying among moving obstacles, and an asteroid landing with minimum-impulse thrusters. We also validate the stability and concentration bounds on a stationkeeping experiment with bounded disturbances.

Sampling-based MPC computes the control input from Monte Carlo rollouts of the dynamics. The path-integral and free-energy formulations were derived in [5, 14], and the receding-horizon MPPI algorithm along with its information-theoretic interpretation was presented in [6, 7, 8]; the underlying importance-sampling estimators are surveyed in [15]. Several methods reduce the rollout dispersion or the model mismatch of MPPI. Tube-MPPI [16] tracks the sampled plan with an ancillary iLQG controller, robust MPPI [17] augments the importance sampler with feedback and analyzes the growth of the free energy, and ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}-adaptive augmentation [18] compensates for matched uncertainty below the sampling rate. Smooth MPPI [19] penalizes the input derivatives, covariance-steering MPPI [20, 21] constrains the terminal rollout dispersion, and gradient-informed or learned proposal distributions [22, 23, 24] reduce the required sample budget. These methods reduce the rollout dispersion or the model mismatch, but the tracking feedback is either applied outside the sampled rollouts or computed from local linearizations without a contraction rate over an explicit domain, and the finite-sample error of the weighted input is not propagated to the closed-loop system. We use the tracking feedback inside every sampled rollout and verify its contraction offline for the nominal nonlinear feedback-closed dynamics over an explicit domain, which keeps the rollouts concentrated around the reference for any horizon. We then propagate the finite-sample error of the weighted input into a stochastic stability bound for the closed-loop system, and we verify the applied input using a DCBF condition, which gives a mission-level probabilistic safety guarantee.

Contraction theory [25, 26] characterizes incremental stability through the variational dynamics, and control contraction metrics [9] extend this analysis to feedback synthesis. In discrete time, the metric can be constructed through Riccati-type recursions [10, 11], and stochastic incremental stability is surveyed in [27]. In predictive control, these certificates are used in tube MPC [28, 29, 30], contraction-based tube planning [31], tubes with cross sections that are adapted online [32], and funnel libraries for sequential composition [33], while more recent work learns the certificates from data [34, 35]. Certified tracking methods that solve a smooth or convexified optimization online cannot use discontinuous costs such as indicators, lookup tables, and ℓ0\ell_{0} costs directly. We use a Riccati-based metric to certify nominal nonlinear contraction on a specified domain, and we use importance sampling to evaluate these costs. As we will discuss, the feedback inside the rollouts also bounds their spread and improves the sample efficiency.

Control barrier functions [36, 37] certify forward invariance of a safe set through a pointwise condition on the control input. The discrete-time conditions are derived in [12], their use within MPC is discussed in [13, 38], nonsmooth compositions using minimum and maximum operations are studied in [39], and predictive safety filters are presented in [40]. In many sampling-based MPC implementations, the barrier appears as a rollout penalty or as a filter on a planned sequence. The admissible input set of a nonlinear barrier can be nonconvex, so that an importance-weighted average of individually feasible sampled inputs need not be feasible, and a rollout penalty does not certify the executed input. Furthermore, stochastic tightening is often derived for temporally independent disturbances, whereas persistent mission parameters can induce prediction errors that are biased and temporally correlated. We verify the barrier condition on the input that is executed. The condition is tightened by a conditional quantile region for the one-step prediction error, which accounts for the persistent mission parameters. If the weighted input does not satisfy the condition, then the controller applies a feasible sampled input or a backup policy (Assumption 5). Under conditional coverage and backup feasibility, we prove the mission-level bound of Proposition 4, which holds for nonsmooth and nonconvex safe sets.

Stochastic MPC [41] handles chance constraints through analytic or scenario-based tightening, learning-based MPC [42, 24] propagates model uncertainty that is estimated from data, and chance-constrained trajectory optimization under stochastic dynamics has been solved using generalized polynomial chaos [43]. These formulations typically compute an open-loop or affine-feedback plan, and their guarantees do not transfer directly when a receding-horizon sampling controller replaces the planned inputs. Many formulations also model temporally independent disturbances, whereas the mission parameters considered in this work persist throughout a trajectory, as in planetary and small-body missions [3, 1, 2, 44]. We state the guarantees for the closed-loop sampling controller. The unobserved mission parameter enters through conditional moments, and the fixed reference can be computed by a standard planning pipeline [45, 46].

We state the problem in Section II and discuss the preliminaries in Section III. In Section IV, we present the CS-MPC method, and in Section V, we derive the concentration and stochastic stability bounds. In Section VI, we validate CS-MPC in simulation on the three examples. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section VII.
